In a post on social media X, the Spanish Confederation of Police (CEP) said on the 'Onda Madrid' radio station, "It is outrageous. Every time there is a crisis Marlaska calls on the police. He knows we are a guarantee of success. But then, as in Ceuta, he punishes us with degrading accommodation that looks like a chamber of horrors."
Overcrowding, heat and a lack of toilets
The officers deployed are reportedly housed in units fitted with eight bunk beds, meaning that seven or eight officers may share a single room, significantly reducing the space available to each officer.
On top of these conditions, officers have complained about the lack of air conditioning in the rooms, in which there is reportedly only one fan for the entire room. This is particularly problematic during the summer months, when the high temperatures in Ceuta make it even harder for officers to get enough rest.
Among the main complaints raised by the officers is the lack of sufficient sanitary facilities. According to information received by the CEP, around 70 officers may be sharing a single toilet on one of the floors of the barracks, a situation which the union considers incompatible with proper hygiene and rest conditions.
In another post on X, commenting for 'Onda Cero' radio, the CEP said, "Colleagues are going to give their all in Ceuta because they are professionals and they know what is at stake there for Spain. Meanwhile, Marlaska punishes them with degrading accommodation, in conditions that would force any minister to resign."
A single bathroom for dozens of officers
Added to this are deficiencies in the showers and ventilation problems in the areas where the officers are being housed. However, the officers make it clear that their criticism is not directed at the military personnel responsible for the facilities.
In fact, the officers themselves highlight the army's willingness to meet their needs within the resources available and speak positively about the treatment they have received during their stay at the barracks.
"We have been treated very well. Top marks to them, but the conditions are what they are and all they have available," the officers say, drawing a distinction between the care and treatment provided by the military personnel and the limitations of the facilities used to house them.
The CEP demands a review of accommodation conditions
In response to the complaints lodged by officers, the CEP has formally requested an urgent preventive inspection to assess, on the ground, the conditions in which police officers deployed to Ceuta are being housed.
The union is specifically calling for a dedicated risk assessment of these facilities to determine whether they meet the necessary safety and health requirements for staff.
As part of this review, the organisation proposes measuring temperature, humidity and ventilation, as well as assessing the conditions of the areas designated for officers to rest.
The CEP insists on the need to objectively verify the shortcomings highlighted by the officers and, if they are confirmed, to apply the necessary corrective measures to guarantee adequate conditions during their time in the city.
The CEP calls for immediate solutions for deployed officers
The CEP is calling for immediate action on the facilities, including upgrading toilets and showers and replacing mattresses that are in poor condition. The union also argues that if the barracks do not meet the required standards, alternative accommodation should be found to ensure decent conditions for the officers deployed.
The organisation stresses that rest and hygiene are particularly important in long deployments, especially when officers have to carry out duties aimed at reinforcing security in the city.
The complaints have already been formally submitted and the CEP expects measures to be taken as soon as possible to remedy the shortcomings and resolve the situation.

Trump administration moves ahead to end roadless rule on national forests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:53:02 UTC
03:53:02 KST

Trump administration moves ahead to end roadless rule on national forests
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — The Trump administration announced Tuesday it is moving ahead with plans to rescind a quarter-century-old rule that blocked logging, road building and other development on national forest lands, drawing the ire of environmentalists nationwide.
The U.S. Forest Service is filing a proposal that would scrap the so called roadless rule adopted in the last days of Bill Clinton’s presidency in 2001. The agency described the rule as a one-size-fits-all restriction that has frustrated land managers and served as a barrier to reducing wildfire risks in the nation’s forests.
“Our forests can’t afford another decade of inaction. Across the country, we’ve watched preventable conditions — overgrown stands, insect outbreaks and disease — turn healthy landscapes into tinderboxes,” U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said in a statement.
Scientists say that worsening wildfires are driven by a combination of climate change that warms and dries out forests, less logging and decades of fire suppression that has allowed fuels to build up.
Clinton had signed the rule to safeguard undeveloped national forest land from commercial logging and mineral leasing, with a goal of keeping ecosystems pristine and protecting water supplies.
Calling the roadless rule a failure, Rollins said the proposal calls for restoring authority to local forest managers and removing barriers that have kept them from improving forest health across millions of acres.
The roadless rule has affected 30% of national forest lands nationwide, or about 59 million acres (24 million hectares), according to the Department of Agriculture, the agency over the Forest Service.
The Forest Service will gather public comment on the proposal and on a draft of the environmental impact statement that was filed Tuesday in the Federal Register. While the rescission removes national designation of roadless areas, officials say it doesn’t mandate timber cutting or road construction.
The filing comes as no surprise as the Trump administration first announced its intention to get rid of the rule during a meeting last summer in New Mexico.
Environmentalists have been sounding the alarm since then and reiterated Tuesday that lifting protections would have detrimental effects for old growth forests, wildlife and water supplies.
“Americans across the political spectrum have made it crystal clear that they don’t want political appointees removing protections from public lands,” said Chris Krupp, an attorney with the group WildEarth Guardians. “It would be a gross misreading of public sentiment to take the roadless rule away from Americans and our wildlife, and politicians do so at their jeopardy.”
Numerous groups raised concerns about what a rescission could mean, especially for places such as Alaska’s Tongass National Forest, the nation’s largest national forest and a lightning rod for litigation. State political leaders there have supported an exemption to the roadless rule that they argue impedes economic opportunities.
During the latter part of Trump’s first term, the federal government lifted restrictions on logging and road-building in the Tongass, something the Biden administration later reversed.
Emma Powell, the Alaska Wilderness League’s government affairs manager, described the Tongass as a global treasure that serves as a home for salmon runs and abundant wildlife. She added that cultures and livelihoods are connected to the forest.
“From fisheries to tourism and outdoor recreation, these landscapes also support thousands of jobs and generate billions in economic activity each year,” Powell said.
Alex Craven, the Sierra Club’s forest campaign manager, disputed officials’ claims that getting rid of the rule would allow for more work to be done to reduce wildfire threats. Craven suggested more roads would lead to more fires and that it never prevented the Forest Service from doing targeted work to reduce wildfire fuels.
He vowed that the Sierra Club and other groups would fight the proposal at each step.
David Jenkins, president of the Virginia-based nonprofit Conservatives for Responsible Stewardship, criticized the proposal as fiscally irresponsible and pointed to an existing maintenance backlog that stretches into the billions of dollars.
“The agency doesn’t have the budget to take care of the 368,000 miles of roads already riddling our national forests,” he said.
The deadline for comments is Sept. 21.

Gambling red flag system under fire as 'Dracula in charge'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:52:04 UTC
03:52:04 KST

Gambling reforms put onus on bookies to flag vulnerable punters
In short:
Wagering companies will have to identify customers showing signs of problem gambling and stop sending them betting inducements.
Critics say allowing the industry to flag its own vulnerable users is too weak, but the federal government says it will curb predatory tactics.
What's next?
Labor's gambling reforms are expected to pass the Senate with the support of the Coalition this week, with detailed criteria of the new red flag inducement system to be developed in the coming months.
Australian wagering companies will identify their own problem gamblers and cut off betting inducements under a system one critic has likened to putting "Dracula in charge of a blood bank".
The plan to let the industry red flag its own vulnerable customers has been labelled weak by advocates who wanted tougher restrictions on the "predatory" tactics, while supporters have described the measure as "significant" reform.
The federal government's gambling ad crackdown passed the lower house on Tuesday and is expected to pass the Senate before the parliament sitting week ends after Labor struck a deal with the Coalition.
Following harrowing evidence about gambling addicts being offered bonus bets and other incentives to gamble being heard at a parliamentary inquiry, the government agreed to curtail so-called inducements.
This included an amendment to create a red flag system where companies are required to tag customers showing signs of problem gambling and stop sending promotions to those individuals.
Liberal MP Andrew Wallace, who was one of two Coalition members to cross the floor and vote against the bill over concerns it was not strong enough, said he did not trust gambling companies to flag potentially lucrative customers.
"I don't think it's acceptable that the bill basically gives [companies] the power to determine whether someone is a problem gambler or not," he said.
"To me, that's like putting Dracula in charge of a blood bank."
In the coming months, existing evidence and research about gambling, such as spend amount, frequency or other betting patterns, will be used to create metrics to guide companies on who they must flag.
Further details like transparency requirements and whether the red flag would be time-limited would also be finalised.
The government would impose the red flag scheme through regulation, with the Australian Media Communications Authority (ACMA) responsible for its enforcement and handling complaints.
Currently, gambling companies are required to identify and respond appropriately to problem behaviour through state and territory regulation, but the national laws would specifically link this work to inducements.
Further restrictions on inducements and TV ads
Further agreed amendments stop companies from marketing inducements to new customers for 14 days from account sign-up, and for three months to people who have come off the self-exclusion register Betstop.
The bill also now bans wagering staff from earning commissions based on customers' gambling activity.
Tackling inducements became a major focus of amendment talks after a Senate inquiry this month heard allegations from NRL player Luke Bateman that gambling company employees unofficially offered to arrange illicit drugs while cultivating relationships with him as a high-volume punter.
The issue was also included in Labor's 2026 national platform endorsed at the party's conference in July.
This week, Labor also agreed to amendments put forward by the Coalition to establish a new opt-out register for gambling advertising, to be called Adstop.
Further changes were also made to extend the ad blackout on television to at least 15 minutes before a live sport game, mirror the broadcast restrictions for streaming platforms and ban ads during children's programming.
The ABC revealed on Monday the gambling agreement had been reached before it was finalised on Tuesday morning with the endorsement of the full Labor caucus and all but a handful of Coalition party room members.
'Incredibly disappointing', says MP who crossed floor
Along with Mr Wallace, Nationals MP Pat Conaghan argued the laws did not go far enough and broke ranks to vote against the gambling bills in the House of Representatives.
Coalition backbenchers are permitted to cross the floor when in opposition if they inform colleagues of their intent, with at least one senator also reserving their right to do the same.
Mr Conaghan, who was on the committee for the online gambling harm inquiry chaired by late Labor MP Peta Murphy three years ago, said it was "incredibly disappointing" many of the recommendations from that report had been "discarded".
"It would have been great to see a national regulator … and to get rid of those inducements online where we heard that evidence from family members of loved ones who had taken their own lives because of the shame and debt," he told Afternoon Briefing.
"I do not live in a bubble; I know it wouldn't have been all 31 recommendations, but the major ones should have been put through.
"Peta Murphy would be incredibly disappointed, and exactly why I crossed the floor for the first time in my career."
Greens say reforms are 'riddled' with holes
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese heralded the legislation as the "most significant gambling advertising reform by any Australian government ever".
"It increases protections for people most at risk of gambling harm, while continuing to allow those who enjoy a bet to do so," he said.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said Labor had listened to a "range of views" across the community and parliament and decided to tackle the "most toxic version" of gambling inducements.
"This package of reforms minimises children's exposure to wagering advertising, takes action on predatory inducements and cracks down on illegal gambling operators," she said.
Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson said the Coalition had negotiated tougher protections where they were needed, while ensuring the laws were "practical, proportionate and respect personal responsibility".
"The Coalition has secured stronger rules around live sport online, children's programs, predatory inducements and the illegal gambling ads flooding social media," she said.
But Greens communications spokeswoman Sarah Hanson-Young said the gambling legislation was "riddled with holes" and criticised Opposition Leader Angus Taylor for making a deal with Mr Albanese.
"The whole bill is a dog, and it's now become a dog's breakfast," she said.
"Angus Taylor has been weak. He's rolled over, and he's yapping like Toto the dog.
"Let's be clear: this is not reform. This is a protection racket for an industry that has lost its social license."
Gambling industry says 'devil will be in the detail'
Responsible Wagering Australia (RWA), a peak industry body for licensed gambling companies, was critical of the amendments made to the bill this week and argued the changes disregard the risk of pushing gamblers to unregulated offshore markets.
RWA chief executive Kai Cantwell said there must be scrutiny of measures that added cost and complexity without a "clear link" to reducing harm.
"The devil will be in the detail, expected to largely be left to regulation."
Mr Cantwell said the complexities of the opt-out advertising register risked undermining the self-exclusion service Betstop and created "serious" implementation concerns.
He said Betstop had taken more than four years to fully implement and questioned how a similar version for all online advertising could be achieved in only four months.
The gambling bill is due to take effect from January 1 next year, but the government is anticipating the Adstop register would take longer to establish
Mr Cantwell said overall the new measures would "significantly curtail" Australian companies' ability to "advertise a legal product safely to adults".
"If you push people away from the licensed, regulated market — by banning or limiting the promotions that let local operators compete, or by making Australian odds less competitive with new taxes and levies — you don't stop them punting," he said.
"You push them offshore, into products with no consumer protections, no support, no Betstop, and no contribution to Australian sport and racing."

Trump administration to rescind rule protecting old-growth forests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:51:47 UTC
03:51:47 KST

The Trump administration said on Tuesday it plans to rescind the “roadless rule” that has protected old-growth forests in the US for 25 years, potentially opening up almost 45m acres of national forests to road construction, drilling and logging.
Conservationists had feared the announcement was coming since last summer after Brooke Rollins, Trump’s secretary of agriculture, targeted a rule brought in by Bill Clinton’s administration, describing it as “overly restrictive” and an “absurd obstacle” to development.
On Tuesday the US Forest Service, an agency inside the Department of Agriculture, formally announced it had filed the proposal to rescind in its entirety the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.
Environmental groups immediately criticized the plan for rollbacks of protections to forests from Alaska to Oregon to North Carolina.
“[The rule] is the only thing preventing much of our wildest remaining national forests from industrial development. These forests offer critical habitat for wildlife, provide clean, fresh air and water for millions and contain vast swathes of the last remaining old-growth forests in the country,” said Alex Craven, forest campaign manager for the Sierra Club.
The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) appealed for submissions for the public comment period to “defend our forests from the administration’s chopping block”.
“Their scheme would open up tens of millions of acres of our national forests to destructive logging, drilling and road building – including iconic public lands from California’s Tahoe national forest to Alaska’s Tongass national forest to the Appalachian Trail,” the NRDC said.
The Trump administration said the move would remove obstacles to managing forests and fighting wildfires.
Rollins said: “For too long, outdated restrictions have kept tens of millions of forested acres off-limits to the very treatments that improve forest health and reduce wildfire risk to our communities.
“Today, we filed a proposal to restore authority to local forest managers who know the land best, removing the barriers that have kept them from doing the work the land demands.”
“Active forest management is not an option. It’s essential,” said Tom Schultz, the forest service chief. “More than 40% of inventoried roadless areas, primarily in the west, have high or very high wildfire hazard potential. And only 5% of those areas have received hazardous fuels reduction treatments since 2014.”
But Craven of the Sierra Club said: “The administration’s attempt to blame the roadless rule for worsening wildfire risk ignores both the facts and the rule itself. Roads generally lead to more ignitions and result in more wildfires – not fewer.
“And, the roadless rule has always allowed for targeted actions to reduce hazardous fuels. What it does not allow is using wildfire as an excuse to open some of America’s most intact public forests to industrial exploitation and new road construction.”
Clinton had championed the roadless rule late in his second term as president after concerns grew around unsustainable logging of national forests.
The biggest roadless area is the Tongass national forest in Alaska, which stores huge amounts of carbon and is home to brown and black bears, wolves and bald eagles.
“America’s last great backcountry forests are not bargaining chips,” Emma Powell, government affairs manager at Alaska Wilderness League, said on Tuesday about the plan. “The Tongass and Chugach national forests are global treasures.
“From fisheries to tourism and outdoor recreation, these landscapes also support thousands of jobs and generate billions in economic activity each year.”
Concerns of environmentalists were especially focussed on logging.
“It’s clear the processes required by the National Environmental Policy Act are being treated as merely boxes to check on the path to enacting an entirely political agenda to clear-cut the last remaining intact old-growth forests in America,” added Maggie Rabb, executive director of the Southeast Alaska Conservation Council.
The public has until 21 September to comment on the plan.
“Trump is pushing for the largest evisceration of public lands protection in American history and against what Americans want,” said Randi Spivak, public lands policy director at the Center for Biological Diversity. “Once you start bulldozing roads for commercial logging and industrial development, there’s no getting them back.”

Bolivia lawmakers likely force economy minister's removal in setback for President Paz

Bolivia lawmakers likely force economy minister's removal in setback for President Paz
LA PAZ, Aug 18 - Bolivia's Congress voted on Tuesday to censure Economy Minister Jose Gabriel Espinoza, a decision President Rodrigo Paz's government said was unconstitutional and signaled would be challenged before the country's top constitutional tribunal.
Presidential spokesperson Jose Luis Galvez said Espinoza could take legal action as soon as Wednesday, suggesting the minister may remain in office while the Constitutional Tribunal reviews the dispute.
Lawmakers backed the motion by majority vote after Espinoza failed to appear before Congress to answer questions on his management of the economy, monetary policy and macroeconomic planning. Espinoza said he had to travel to the city of Santa Cruz to address diesel supply problems before heading to Brazil.
The minister said on Tuesday that he would turn to the nation's top constitutional tribunal to review the decision, arguing that procedures may have been violated.
Under Bolivia's constitution, Paz has 24 hours to remove a censured minister from office. But the government argues the censure vote did not meet constitutional requirements and that the issue should be reviewed by the Constitutional Tribunal before Espinoza is removed.
The dispute raises the stakes in a confrontation between Paz and lawmakers at a delicate moment for his economic reform agenda.
"Tomorrow, the minister in question will take the appropriate actions and may eventually exercise his rights under the Constitution; however, the call is for all procedures to be conducted in accordance with the Constitution," Galvez said.
Galvez said the vote fell short of the constitutional requirement for censure, which he said requires a two-thirds majority, or 111 votes, of the 166-member Congress. Only 91 lawmakers voted to censure Espinoza.
"Any censure resolution issued based on these results is unconstitutional," Galvez said, arguing that internal congressional rules cannot override the constitution.
REFORM AGENDA AT STAKE
The vote comes at a sensitive time for Paz's government, which is seeking congressional backing for economic reforms and for a financing program negotiated with the International Monetary Fund in July that still requires approval from both Bolivia's Congress and the IMF Executive Board.
The program is seen as key to helping stabilize the economy and easing persistent shortages of fuel and foreign currency.
Espinoza said his dismissal reflected "extreme" politicization and cited clashes between the government's work agenda and lawmakers' timelines.
Espinoza has been part of Paz's government since the administration took office in November and has become one of the main architects of the government's economic policy. He has also played a central public role in negotiations with multilateral lenders.
In recent weeks, Espinoza also faced criticism over the alleged purchase of an Audi vehicle at a declared price well below market value. Espinoza said the discrepancy was the result of a paperwork error. REUTERS

Russian Jet-Powered ‘Shahed’ Drone Reaches Western Ukraine for First Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:47:00 UTC
03:47:00 KST

A Russian jet-powered “Shahed” drone flew approximately 900 kilometers (nearly 560 miles) from its launch point in Crimea into western Ukraine on Tuesday, Aug. 18, marking the farthest such strike recorded so far.
According to the eRadar monitoring channel, which conducted a detailed analysis of the drone’s flight, the drone traveled from Crimea through Mykolaiv, Vinnytsia, and Khmelnytskyi regions before passing near Kremenets in the Ternopil region and eventually reaching the city of Dubno in the Rivne region.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The drone covered a distance of 850 to 920 kilometers (roughly 528 to 572 miles) when accounting for maneuvering, with a straight-line penetration depth of more than 720 kilometers (about 447 miles) from its launch point.
“Today’s tracked route of an enemy jet-powered drone is a clear demonstration of how the enemy is testing our air defense system and searching for new corridors using jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs),” eRadar said.
A route built to avoid air defenses
The drone’s transit through southern, central, and western Ukraine indicates the route “was calculated in advance to avoid the main deployment areas” of Ukraine’s anti-aircraft missile systems, eRadar said.
The monitoring group described this as evidence that Russia is actively searching for “blind spots” in the country’s air defense network, rather than flying a direct line toward a fixed target.
Ukraine, Belgium Advance Talks on Drone Deal
According to RBC-Ukraine, citing Rivne Regional Military Administration head Oleksandr Koval, an aerial target – likely the same type of jet-powered drone – was shot down over the southern part of the region.
The interception came after Ukraine’s Air Force tracked the drone crossing multiple regions over the course of roughly 30 minutes.
Speed complicating ground defense
The drone’s jet engine, which reaches speeds of 400 to 600 kilometers per hour (roughly 249 to 373 miles per hour), significantly reduces the chances of interception, particularly using small arms or large-caliber machine guns.
“Therefore, ‘classic’ mobile fire groups are completely impractical in this case,” eRadar said.
Until now, jet-powered drones had a typical operational range of up to 500 kilometers (around 310 miles), which limited their use largely to regions such as Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa, Sumy, Poltava, Dnipropetrovsk, and the Chernihiv region, RBC-Ukraine reported.
Tuesday’s flight nearly doubled that distance, suggesting Russia has modified its drone models to extend their range.
Broader implications
The extended range means that “virtually the entire territory of Ukraine – right up to its most remote western borders” now falls within the zone of possible Russian strikes, eRadar said.
According to a separate report from the Institute for the Study of War on Monday, Aug. 17, Russia is expanding its network of drone launch sites, with western Ukraine emerging as a likely future target.
Speaking on Monday, Anton Zemlyanyi, a senior analyst at the Ukrainian Center for Security and Cooperation said Russia is increasingly relying on faster drones as the effectiveness of conventional Shaheds in large-scale attacks declines.

To Putin’s delight: Politicians in Poland and Ukraine are stoking mutual hostility for the sake of their ratings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:45:26 UTC
03:45:26 KST

In early 2022, when Russian tanks were massed outside Kyiv, Poland proved to be one of Ukraine’s most reliable and steadfast allies. But four years later, relations have entered a crisis — one fueled by historical grievances and economic disputes. Today, 52% of Poles are opposed to their country supporting Ukraine’s accession to the EU, while 44% favor suspending military aid. Politicians on both sides of the border are actively exploiting these disagreements to boost their own ratings, forgetting about the strategic partnership. Meanwhile, Russia is gleefully fanning the flames of the dispute, Polish commentator Pavel Reshka writes.
Family quarrels
What is happening today at the level of the Polish and Ukrainian governments sometimes resembles a kindergarten sandbox squabble. For example, Polish politicians recently began competing over who had sent less military equipment to Ukraine.
“We gave them nothing but scrap metal from our warehouses!” says a former prime minister.
“Scrap metal? It was pretty good weaponry! I’ll show everyone the documents now! Here we are! We’re hardly giving them anything,” counters the former defense minister.
“What about the Patriot missiles?” the opposition presses.
Under normal circumstances, a cabinet minister would be proud of having sent missiles to save the lives of countless innocent civilians by protecting Ukraine from Russia’s barbaric attacks. But now this is not a source of pride, but a political problem — something that requires defensive justification.
Or take the Ukrainian president naming a Ukrainian Armed Forces unit after the “heroes of the UPA.” This, in fact, was the initial trigger of the current escalation. Volodymyr Zelenskyy showed complete disregard for the fact that the reaction in Poland would be fierce, as the awful role of the WWII-era Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) in the Volhynia Massacre represents a historical wound that has still not healed. When pollsters ask Poles, “What should the government discuss with Ukraine?” they hear in response: the exhumation and commemoration of the thousands of compatriots killed by the UPA in 1943, who still lie in the ground in mass graves on the other side of the border.
Moves like Zelensky's provoke outrage. Polish President Karol Nawrocki, egged on by pro-Russian politicians such as former Prime Minister Leszek Miller, demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy be stripped of the Order of the White Eagle. (gov.pl)
Zelensky did not keep him waiting long, sending it back to Nawrocki by mail in a box, and several former Ukrainian presidents, cabinet ministers, ambassadors, and officials followed suit with their Polish awards. Suddenly, a multitude of Orders of the White Eagle arrived in Poland. In the opposite direction, Polish officials sent Orders of Prince Yaroslav the Wise, 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Class.
Warsaw is not at the table during “Coalition of the Willing” meetings — at Kyiv’s behest — nor is it part of the newly formed anti-ballistic coalition.
“Fine! We don’t care. And you’re not getting into the EU with your Bandera anyway,” the Poles say.
“You don’t care? Well, did you know Zelensky won’t be coming to Gdańsk?”
“But it’s the Ukraine Recovery Conference!”
“We can handle the recovery without you as well.”
Online, the two sides are trading blows. Experts and analysts on the Polish side are sounding the alarm that Ukraine is steeped in Nazism and Bandera ideology. Ukrainian experts insist that the atmosphere in Poland is reminiscent of the period before pogroms. They call on fellow citizens living along the Vistula to return home (which makes sense, since Ukraine has an interest in having its citizens return, just as Polish business owners have an interest in having them stay in Poland).
It should be noted here that the Polish police respond firmly and in an exemplary manner to reports of physical aggression against Ukrainians (these are orders from above). However, anti-Ukrainian and anti-Polish sentiment is currently in vogue – it generates clicks and likes.
The conflict has gone so far that Przemysław Czarnek, a leading politician in Poland’s main opposition party, Law and Justice (PiS), and a potential candidate for prime minister, declares: “We need to force the European Union, including by using our position within the EU, to suspend all funding for arms deliveries to Ukraine and for Ukraine’s reconstruction for the time being, until it sets out on the path of universal human values.”
True, Czarnek was called to order by the party chairman and the party split — not surprising given that PiS is not some fringe group, but the main opposition party. It was PiS that was running Poland in 2022 and did everything it could to help its neighbors. Its political position has always been to support Ukraine’s sovereignty and exercise caution toward imperial Russia. Its ranks produced the late Lech Kaczyński, who addressed the parliament in Tbilisi in 2008, with Russian tanks stationed on the outskirts of the city: “Today Georgia, tomorrow Ukraine, the day after tomorrow the Baltic states, and then perhaps the time will come for my country, Poland!” Now, one of the leading figures in the PiS of 2026 is calling for the suspension of Western aid to Kyiv.
Pendulum: from love to hatred
Amid the flurry of mutual accusations, several fundamental problems are being overlooked. Ukraine is fighting a defensive war. At such a moment, its only concern is the struggle for survival. When you are fighting for your life, there is no room for any phrase beginning with “yes, but…” There are no nuances when the world is burning, bombs are falling on your head, and the eastern horde is taking yet another village.
There are no nuances when the world is burning, bombs are falling on your head, and the eastern horde is taking yet another city
Poland is Ukraine’s closest ally. Whatever politicians and commentators in Warsaw may say, it is a weapons supplier and the logistical backbone of the front.
The two countries have a common existential enemy, and Ukraine’s defeat would be a catastrophe for Poland’s security. Ukraine’s victory and its continued course toward the West are crucial to that security, but Ukraine will not ever be able to join the EU without Poland’s consent. And glorifying historical figures who are, to put it mildly, controversial, certainly does not help Kyiv's cause. More than a million Ukrainians live, work, study, and pay taxes in Poland. Despite the disagreements, we are neighbors. And as we can see, despite the Kremlin’s enormous efforts, that is not going to change.
In the words of Jerzy Giedroyc, whose ideas became the foundation of Poland’s foreign policy after 1989:
“Polish state interests require a belt of independent states between Poland and Russia. Warsaw should support the sovereignty of its eastern neighbors, even if this means giving up some historical claims and disputes. Historical conflicts with Ukrainians should not obscure the strategic goal – an independent Ukraine as a guarantee of Poland’s security against Russian imperialism.”
So what, then, is the problem? Well, if you look at it coldly and armed with statistics, there is nothing surprising about the current dispute. CBOS, one of Poland’s most important public opinion research centers, first asked respondents about their attitudes toward Ukrainians in 1993. At the time, just 12% of Poles expressed sympathy for their neighbors, while a full 65% of respondents expressed dislike. Even Russians, Germans, and Jews – nations that traditionally receive only “so-so” affection in Poland – elicited warmer feelings. One could say that Poles really enjoyed not liking Ukrainians back then. A year later, in 1994, sympathy fell even further, reaching a historic low of 9%.
And all this was happening at a time when the Third Polish Republic was proud that “Solidarity” had helped bring down the USSR – the evil empire. In Warsaw, the independence gained by every nation recently subjugated under Moscow's rule was greeted with applause. On a diplomatic level, Poland was, after all, the first country to recognize Ukraine’s independence. The ideas of Jerzy Giedroyc described above were the guiding principle of its eastern policy, even if the mood in society was less than enthusiastic about befriending their newly free neighbor.
Interestingly, in the years that followed, sympathy toward Ukrainians and Ukraine slowly grew — albeit in an up-and-down pattern resembling a sine wave creeping upward. Surges of warm feelings came at particular moments. Poles felt warmly toward their neighbors in 2004 during the Orange Revolution, in 2008 at the time of the Russian-Georgian war, and in 2013–2014 during Ukraine's Revolution of Dignity, Russia's annexation of Crimea, and the outbreak of war in Donbas. Each upswing was followed by a cooling-off period, usually caused by fatigue with the situation and the return of difficult questions about history, particularly the war crimes committed by the UPA in Volhynia.
For a long time, Ukrainian politicians considered the UPA issue to be a problem invented for the purposes of domestic politics in Poland. However, as all the studies show, this is a deep wound that cannot be ignored. In 1943, at least 100,000 innocent civilians were killed in mass killings organized by the UPA. They were murdered in brutal ways. To this day, many Poles believe that the matter has not been properly resolved, and it cannot be buried without exhumations and re-burials. Ukraine blocked a decision on this for years.
The killing of 100,000 Polish civilians by the UPA cannot be resolved without exhumations and burials, and Ukraine blocked a decision on this for years
Thus, Poles' sympathy for their neighbors rose and fell. However, the pendulum never returned to its previous position, and from decade to decade, Poles grew increasingly fond of Ukrainians. By around 2010, sympathy had even begun to outweigh antipathy.
Sentiments on the other side of the border were similar. This is only natural: when we are in trouble, we appreciate a neighbor who wants to come to our aid, and we are grateful to them. Polish flags on the Maidan, the visit of Presidents Lech Kaczyński and Viktor Yushchenko to Tbilisi in 2008, Warsaw’s protests against the brazen annexation of Crimea – all this made a favorable impression on Ukrainians.
A pattern is easy to spot here: the worse Russian behavior was, the better relations between Poles and Ukrainians became. From this perspective, their attachment was a function of their dislike of an aggressive neighbor that threatened “both you and us.” A similar mechanism came into play in 2022. Poles opened their homes and hearts, taking in hundreds of thousands of women and children fleeing the full-scale war unleashed by the Kremlin.
President Andrzej Duda, the PiS government, and the opposition alike did everything they could to provide civilians with social assistance and the Ukrainian army with weapons and ammunition. However, the wave of spontaneous empathy and outrage at Russia, which was committing war crimes, did not prevent Polish politicians from keeping an eye on sociological trends. They could see that if Ukraine survived, the pendulum of sympathy would begin to swing in the other direction, and they needed to prepare for that.
Sociologists say that 2022 was nevertheless such an extraordinary year that it completely disrupted the typical pattern on both sides of the border. CBOS polls show that in March of that year, 94% of Poles supported accepting refugees from Ukraine, and Poland was Ukrainians’ most favored country, with 83% expressing a positive opinion of Poles. President Zelensky said that Ukraine and Poland were sisters.
It must be said that sister Poland really did open its arms wide to sister Ukraine. Legislators in Warsaw changed laws with lightning speed: for example, the law on assistance to Ukrainian citizens was adopted as early as March 12, 2022. This allowed refugees to easily legalize their stay and establish lives thanks to access to the labor market, social assistance, health care, and education – around 300,000 children and teenagers who did not know the language entered the school system. The challenge was enormous: during the first two weeks after February 24 alone, around a million people crossed the Polish border. Europe had not seen such a mass movement since World War II.
And estimates of the size of the migration varied considerably. For example, according to the Union of Polish Metropolises, shortly after the invasion there could have been as many as 3.9 million Ukrainians in Poland.
Reality and emotions
A year and a half later, more precise estimates could be made. They showed that the number of Ukrainians in Poland with an active PESEL Ukr number (which confirms legal residence and grants access to social benefits) stood at around 970,000. The majority of them (87%) were women and children. Poland is also home to more than 420,000 Ukrainians residing on other grounds, including temporary residence related to employment and permanent residence. This puts the total at approximately 1.4 million.
Sister Ukraine actively got to work in Poland. A year and a half after the invasion, 80% of Ukrainian migrant households supported themselves through their own labor. They worked for others or started businesses themselves: since 2022, Ukrainians have founded 60,000 businesses, of which around 35,000 remain active. They also own or co-own the largest share of companies with foreign capital (41%). “Ukrainian workers contributed to higher economic growth, by between 0.7 and 1.1 percentage points,” says Aleksander Łaszek, PhD in economics and a Deloitte expert.
Sister Poland, however, was in shock. After World War II, our country was essentially mono-ethnic. According to the 2011 National Census, foreigners accounted for only 0.1–0.2% of Poland’s population, or about 60,000 people. In reality, the figure was probably closer to 100,000, but hearing another language on the street was something unusual. In recent years, everything has been turned upside down: Ukrainian, and less often Russian and Belarusian, can be heard in stores, hospitals, and hotels. This could not fail to provoke a reaction from a society unprepared for such a dramatic change, and its effects were bound to begin showing up in the polls.
According to the 2011 National Population Census, foreigners accounted for around 0.1–0.2% of Poland’s population
Symptoms of the unraveling solidarity appeared fairly early. “What united the narratives of our middle- and working-class respondents was a strong dislike of Ukrainians, expressed spontaneously in all the focus groups. They reflect anxiety about losing priority access to benefits and public services,” Przemysław Sadura and Sławomir Sierakowski wrote in their report "Poles Are for Ukraine, but Against Ukrainians," based on research conducted in early June 2022.
Such voices rarely broke through into public discourse, but in real life people increasingly talked, for example, about Ukrainians driving down wages. The actual data showed that this was not true. For example, the influx of migrants had a negligible effect on the rise in unemployment (0.18–0.3%), and as Dr. Łaszek noted, “A Ukrainian taking a job was often associated with a Polish worker being promoted because they were more experienced and had a better command of the language.”
However, some rumors cannot be disproved with hard economic data. How, for example, do you disprove the panicked rumors about cunning Ukrainian women who, instead of showing gratitude, set about seducing Polish husbands? Or about Ukrainian children being admitted to emergency departments (SORs) ahead of young Poles waiting in line? These stories spread on social media, and according to experts, they were part of a disinformation campaign – one of many that would later sweep across Poland.
Of course, there were also measurable, entirely objective factors. Ukraine, having gained easier access to EU markets for grain and transportation because of the ongoing war, became a genuine competitor to Polish farmers and businesses. This resulted in a huge influx of grain into Poland, falling prices, and farmers’ protests in 2023, accompanied by a blockade of the border and Ukrainian grain being dumped onto the ground – images that were particularly painful in Ukraine, which had experienced the Holodomor.
This was compounded by President Zelensky’s words at a UN session: “Some of our friends are helping to set the stage for a Moscow actor.” In Poland, this was perceived as a stab in the back to President Andrzej Duda, who was finding it increasingly difficult to rally his camp behind unconditional support for Ukraine.
Moreover, Ukraine was putting pressure on EU institutions, arguing that the restrictions were hurting its economy and violating the principles of the single market and trade agreements. The European Commission became an arena for the dispute, as it was the Commission that administered the so-called autonomous trade measures for Ukraine. In September 2023, after the Commission decided not to extend the EU ban on imports, Ukraine filed a complaint against Poland (and also against Hungary and Slovakia) at the WTO.
In Poland, this was seen as disloyalty and a lack of solidarity. After all, it was not only Andrzej Duda who might have disliked Zelensky’s barbed hint at him in his UN speech. The late Lech Kaczyński must have felt awful when his friend Viktor Yushchenko called Stepan Bandera and Roman Shukhevych heroes. And Bronisław Komorowski must have felt the same when, on the day he addressed the Verkhovna Rada, Ukrainian lawmakers passed a law granting UPA fighters veteran status.
Foreign policy as domestic policy
Poland entered an electoral cycle in 2023, beginning with parliamentary elections marked by the highest turnout in the country's history. This was followed by the no less hotly contested presidential election of 2025. In 2027 there will once again be a battle for a parliamentary majority, a fact that does not make for normal debate.
Parties commission polls and tailor their messaging to voters’ expectations, and a combination of fear and anxiety can propel a party to the top. Everyone wants to ride this wave; no one will swim against the current, because they will drown.
“Of course, politicians sensed the growing skepticism and did not want to go against the tide,” political scientist Ernest Wyciszkiewicz, until recently the director of the Juliusz Mieroszewski Center for Dialogue, said in an interview with Polityka weekly. The center has been conducting detailed sociological research on Polish-Ukrainian relations since the beginning of the invasion, and historical issues — Volhynia, exhumations, and irritation over monuments being erected and streets being named after figures such as UPA commander Roman Shukhevych — have been coming up increasingly often.
On the Ukrainian side, meanwhile, there has been a noticeable rise in national pride. There has also been a renaissance of interest in history. Under the circumstances of the war, the past actions of the UPA have been reinterpreted. Just a decade and a half ago, only around 20% of respondents viewed the UPA positively. Today, the overwhelming majority viewing them as fighters for independence. More than 80% sympathize with Stepan Bandera, and around 70% with Roman Shukhevych, both of whom are viewed as villains in Poland.
More than 80% of Ukrainians sympathize with Bandera, and around 70% with Shukhevych
Poles do not like this, but this is perhaps the worst possible moment to give their neighbors “history lessons.” Ukrainians are defending themselves against Russia and suffering daily casualties. They have no desire to listen to criticism from anyone.
At the same time, far-right groups have been gaining popularity in Poland by riding the anti-Ukrainian wave. A party called “Confederation” received 7% and 18 seats in parliament in October 2023, finishing fifth. Today, “Confederation” has split into two factions, both of which are gaining ground: the first has around 13–15% support, while the second has around 8–11%. In the presidential election, candidates from “Confederation” came in third and fourth, while the top spot went to PiS candidate Karol Nawrocki, a former head of the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) who had no qualms about attacking “Banderite” Ukraine, threatening that it would not join NATO or the EU and calling for the “restoration of justice” – that is, stripping refugees of financial benefits.
The radicals’ convictions inevitably set the tone of the debate, leading others to become more radical. As a result, a law was passed abolishing assistance for the most vulnerable Ukrainian refugees who depend on aid. It is not about the money (after all, it is a pittance), but about showing that we care primarily about our own citizens. The prime minister talks about the need to deport young Ukrainians who got into a scuffle with security guards at a concert (by Max Korzh in Warsaw), while the interior minister personally takes up the case of a blogger who drove a race car with Ukrainian license plates into a national park in the Tatra Mountains to take a selfie. The illegal catching of a catfish by a Ukrainian migrant is elevated to the level of a national security issue.
Ukraine, too, pretends that it is not engaged in domestic politics amid the war, but that is not true either. A political game is afoot in Kyiv given the understanding that as soon as the shooting stops, parliamentary elections and a new race for the presidency will begin.
A Ukrainian opposition politician said that viewing the current dispute with Poland as a cunning ploy by Zelensky would be a gross exaggeration: “There is a narrative being promoted in Warsaw that Zelensky cleverly engineered all this – he stirred up a storm and boosted his ratings. That is a wonderful compliment to the president’s entourage, but completely undeserved. There was no plan. It should be added that, like a stage performer, he has a genius for reading his audience. He quickly realized that people liked this assertiveness and went in that direction: ‘Karol wants the White Eagle back? Great, send it!’ And he was right. The support was enormous. Unfortunately, the price was a deterioration in relations with Poland.”
Zelensky went further, pushing through a law on the Pantheon of Heroes of Ukraine. It is to be a place commemorating figures important to the country’s history and will almost certainly include people whom Warsaw will find difficult to accept. Kyiv, for example, is seeking the return of Stepan Bandera’s remains to Ukraine, to be followed by a ceremonial burial. Even politicians who are not sympathetic to Zelensky came out in his support.
Zelensky is, after all, fighting for reelection. A huge corruption scandal is hanging over him, and increasingly serious opponents are emerging. The situation at the front, dissatisfaction with mobilization, and holes in the budget are all on his shoulders. Relations with Poland are certainly not a priority for him. Preserving his hold on power, however, is.
Nothing but negativity
The Polish research group Res Futura, which studies the internet and social media, noticed something interesting during the latest dispute over naming a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA.” According to its research, 754,000 posts about Ukraine appeared from June 1-21, 2026. These posts generated 10.2 million reactions and comments. “Among non-neutral posts, nine out of ten are negative toward Ukrainians,” emphasized Michał Fedorowicz of Res Futura.
Between June 1 and 21, 2026, 754,000 posts about Ukraine appeared, and if neutral posts are excluded, nine out of ten are negative, Res Futura calculated
Criticism of Ukraine on social media has been growing steadily since the beginning of May, and each crisis pushes this level higher. Importantly, it no longer recedes.
Fedorowicz says that the UPA issue accounted for less than 5% of discussions about Ukraine on social media a year ago. At the time, there was a social and online consensus that the issue should not be discussed because it served Russia’s interests (and was being promoted by pro-Russian propaganda). However, the situation has now been turned upside down: “Today, there is absolutely no room – above all, politically – to change these sentiments.”
Of course, eventually, the pendulum will swing in the other direction again – the sooner, the better. At some point, Poland and Ukraine will love each other a little more again – they have little choice. That is, after all, how sisters love.

US Amb. Huckabee doubles down on 'terror' label for Israeli occupier violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:45:14 UTC
03:45:14 KST

Yasin Gungor
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
The US Amb. to Israel, Mike Huckabee, reaffirmed his condemnation Tuesday of extremist occupier violence in the occupied West Bank, asserting that the actions meet the American definition of terrorism.
“Once it involves an American citizen, then our involvement is pretty much automatic and it's going to be significant because that's our job,” Huckabee told Channel 12 in Israel. He noted that while Washington would otherwise only express concerns, the targeting of an American’s home in Qusra necessitated direct involvement.
Huckabee, a staunch ally of Israel, rejected pushback from Israeli officials about his terminology. “I’ll use the word terror,” he said, explaining that any act intended to put individuals in fear for their lives or force behavioral changes constitutes terrorism under US law. He emphasized that it applies whether the targets are nations, families, or specific individuals.
The remarks follow a siege of Palestinian homes in Qusra by Israeli occupiers, including one belonging to a dual US citizen. Earlier this month, the UN warned that violence by occupiers had reached unprecedented levels, reporting more than 1,430 attacks on Palestinians and their property since the start of 2026.
 
Political engagement, neutrality
Huckabee also provided insight as to why US President Donald Trump stopped short of endorsing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel's elections.
“I think he's sensitive. He doesn't want to engage,” said Huckabee, noting that the US president carefully weighs whether his involvement would be "helpful" or "hurtful." He suggested that Trump might refrain from an endorsement if he believes it could "tip the scale unfairly," though he emphasized that Trump remains a leader who speaks his mind when he deems it necessary.
Trump acknowledged that he would “most likely” endorse Netanyahu, but said he would have to see first who he was running against.
The ambassador also confirmed he is actively seeking to meet with a broad range of Israeli political figures, including opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot. Huckabee said that he intends to meet with "as many as is humanly possible," despite the complexity of the fluctuating political party landscape.

Swedish MP intervenes in ‘damaging’ Brexit row over elderly Britons ordered to leave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:44:06 UTC
03:44:06 KST

The deportation and removal of British citizens from Sweden over Brexit residency rights is damaging relations with the UK amid efforts to improve links with London, a Swedish MP has said.
Häkan Svenneling, representative for Vârmland, where a 78-year-old British widow, Joyce Thomas, has been given four weeks to leave Sweden after 21 years of residency, has written to the migration minister, Johan Forssell, asking what he “intends to do to stop the deportations”.
Sevenneling, who is an opposition MP for the left, is to meet Thomas on Wednesday, exactly a week after she was told her appeal had failed over the removal order.
Thomas told the Guardian: “I am in shock. I feel sick. An individual’s life is at stake at my age. It is hell. I have done nothing wrong.”
The retired nurse moved to Sweden with her financier husband, to be closer to one of their sons and their grandchildren, when she was 57.
Her husband, who died of cancer in 2023, did all the administrative work in the household, but both Thomas and her friends have said repeatedly they checked if they had to complete any forms to remain in the country after Brexit, and were told they did not.
Thomas made a late application to remain in Sweden in 2023, just weeks after they returned from the UK, but missing the deadline of 31 December 2021. She and her friends testify that her husband checked whether Brexit was going to affect their residency and they were told they did not need to do anything.
Thomas, who is self sufficient and is not drawing benefit from the Swedish state, has spoken of the “hell” she is now in with the threat of imminent removal, separating her from her family, strong network of friends, and her husband’s grave.
Svenneling says in his letter to Forssell that Britons lawfully in Sweden before the UK’s exit from the EU would see their “existing residency rights continue to apply” under the withdrawal agreement (W/A).
“It was not intended to result in elderly people who had lived in Sweden for decades losing their rights to remain because of a missed deadline or deficiencies in their application [to stay],” he said.
Svenneling’s written parliamentary question adds to growing pressure on the prime minister, Ulf Kristersson’s, centre-right minority coalition to address increasing concerns over the way Sweden is implementing the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, an international, legally binding, treaty.
“The United Kingdom has long been an important partner for Sweden in a wide range of areas. It is clear that the deportations now taking place are damaging bilateral relations between Sweden and the United Kingdom,” Svenneling said.
He raised the case of Thomas, but also of another elderly Briton, Horace (George) Mason, 74, who has dementia and Parkinson’s and is in full-time care. Thomas moved to Sweden 25 years ago to be closer to his son Carl and his grandchildren. He, too, was given four weeks to leave.
His family tried a second legal route for him to remain in Sweden, arguing he had rights, under the European conventionon human rights, to stay close to family on whom he relied. But the migration court of appeal ruled that “the state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs Mason’s interest in continuing to reside” in Sweden.
Writing in the Guardian, David Milstead, who heads the campaign group Brits in Sweden, said the group raised the alarm over Sweden’s approach as far back as 2020 and the safeguards put in place were “untested”.
“Among genuine missed-deadline cases brought to our 9,000-member group, we cannot verify one in which Sweden accepted the reasons for applying late,” he said.
The UK Foreign Office said it has repeatedly raised concerns with the European Commission “that Sweden is taking a considerably stricter approach” to late applications than any other EU member state, with a disproportionate number of refusals.
It said it appeared that “in practice, individuals are not likely to have their reasonable grounds [for a late application] accepted”.
Milstead is concerned that Sweden’s wider migration policy could be affecting decisions made under the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, and has called on the European Commission and Sweden to urgently address the issues.
“Sweden’s migration politics have moved sharply towards restriction. That cannot displace EU law, but it makes remedial action harder to defend politically,” he said.
The migration agency in Sweden said it was unable to discuss individual cases, but that not knowing a Brexit application had to be made to remain in the country was not a “reasonable ground” to stay.

Russian missile strike hits center of Pechenihy in Ukraine’s northeastern Kharkiv Region, killing 10 and wounding 17
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:43:12 UTC
03:43:12 KST

A Russian missile strike on the town of Pechenihy in Ukraine’s Kharkiv Region on the morning of Aug. 18 killed 10 people and wounded 17 others, according to a report by regional military administration head Oleh Syniehubov. Ukrainian authorities said the strike hit the center of the town, where cafes, a post office, and shops are located.
Fourteen of the wounded were hospitalized, while three others received treatment at the scene, Viktor Zabashta, director of the regional emergency medical center, told Suspilne, Ukraine’s public broadcaster. The wounded suffered burns and shrapnel injuries, and some are in serious condition. Syniehubov said DNA testing would be needed to identify the dead.
Oleksandr Husarov, head of the Pechenihy community, said Russian forces attacked the town with two Banderol missiles. The two munitions landed about 50 meters apart, with one striking a cafe. Among those killed, Husarov said, were customers, vendors, and people who were nearby. Work to clear the rubble is continuing, meaning the casualty figures could rise.
The attack damaged 10 private homes, a cafe, a post office, a shop, and at least seven cars. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the strike hit a “crowded intersection” surrounded by residential buildings. A fire at the site was extinguished.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, classifies the S8000 Banderol as a Russian cruise missile that is developed and produced by the Russian company Kronshtadt. It has a range of up to 500 kilometers and a maximum speed of 620 to 650 kilometers per hour. Among other components, the missile uses a Chinese turbojet engine and foreign-made electronics.

Cargo ship damaged in attack off Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:35:54 UTC
03:35:54 KST

ALBAWABA- A cargo ship was damaged after coming under attack in the southern Red Sea off Yemen, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported on Tuesday, as Houthi attacks on commercial and Saudi-linked vessels continue to raise concerns over maritime security in the Bab al-Mandab region.
UKMTO said it received a report of an incident approximately 40 nautical miles southeast of Al-Makha, also known as Mocha, on Yemen’s Red Sea coast. Initial reports indicated that the vessel was struck by an unknown projectile, causing damage. Further details about the ship, the nature of the attack and any casualties were not immediately available. UKMTO advised vessels operating in the area to exercise caution.
The latest incident comes amid a sharp escalation in Houthi maritime operations along Yemen’s western coast. On August 11, a small commercial vessel was attacked in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing crew members. Yemeni authorities and international reports said six people were ultimately killed in the attack, including three Pakistani nationals and one Indonesian, while several others were injured. Two rescuers were also killed when the vessel was attacked again after rescue teams arrived.
The attack was followed by further Houthi operations against shipping and maritime infrastructure. On Monday, the Houthis claimed they had attacked what they described as a Saudi military vessel and four escort ships with missiles off Mocha. Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed the claim.
The group has also expanded its declared maritime campaign against Saudi-linked shipping. In July, the Houthis announced what they described as a maritime blockade targeting Saudi-bound vessels, saying the measure was in response to what they called a Saudi blockade of Yemen. They subsequently claimed attacks against Saudi oil tankers, including vessels transiting the Red Sea.
The escalation has coincided with renewed fighting between the Houthis and forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government. The United Nations has warned that Yemen is facing its most serious risk of a return to large-scale conflict since the 2022 truce, citing increased military activity and clashes in areas including Marib, Hadramawt and the western coast. The renewed fighting has also increased the risk that Yemen’s internal conflict could become more deeply connected to the wider regional confrontation.
Mocha has emerged as one of the main flashpoints. The port, located close to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, has been repeatedly targeted in recent Houthi attacks. Port authorities said on August 15 that more than 25 missiles had struck the facility over several days, killing seven people and causing an estimated $16 million in damage. The attacks forced the port to suspend commercial and maritime operations.
The attacks have severely disrupted a strategically important coastal hub used by anti-Houthi forces and commercial operators. The port’s closure has further complicated maritime activity along a waterway that connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and provides one of the world's key routes for shipping between Europe and Asia.
The latest reported attack also highlights the increasingly complex security environment facing commercial vessels in the region. The Houthis have sought to link their maritime operations to developments involving Saudi Arabia and the broader regional conflict, while anti-Houthi forces have intensified military operations along the western coast. The resulting cycle of attacks and counterattacks has increased risks for both commercial shipping and civilian infrastructure.
The situation is particularly significant because the Bab al-Mandab is a critical international shipping chokepoint. Any sustained disruption could force vessels to divert around the Cape of Good Hope, increasing voyage times, fuel costs and insurance premiums. The renewed attacks therefore threaten not only Yemen’s fragile security situation but also the reliability of an important global trade route.
The latest UKMTO report comes as maritime tensions are simultaneously escalating elsewhere in the region, including around the Strait of Hormuz, where commercial shipping has faced growing threats amid the wider confrontation involving Iran, the United States and Gulf states. The simultaneous pressure on the two strategic waterways has heightened concerns that regional conflicts could increasingly affect international maritime trade.

OpenAI Overhauls Safety Protocols After Its AI Agents Went Rogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:33:11 UTC
03:33:11 KST

OpenAI announced Tuesday that it has halted “a significant number” of training workloads and evaluations for its forthcoming frontier artificial intelligence model—codenamed Astra—while it implements new procedures meant to address cybersecurity risks. The ChatGPT maker says it is introducing a number of new monitoring, security, and alignment requirements to better address the increasingly advanced hacking abilities of its frontier AI models.
“We have to focus our energy on bringing these training runs up to those requirements and expectations. As long as it takes to get there, that's how long people are unable to proceed with their workloads,” Amelia Glaese, OpenAI’s vice president of research and safety, said in a briefing with reporters Tuesday.
Among the new safeguards OpenAI announced is a more robust system for monitoring its AI models. One of the controls it implemented involves chain-of-thought monitoring, a technique in which classifiers review the internal “thinking” processes generated by AI reasoning models. The company says the updated system relies on computationally expensive “automated investigators” that analyze potentially concerning behavior and aim to issue an alert to humans within 30 minutes.
OpenAI also said it is expanding its alignment efforts across the training process to prevent “reward hacking,” a behavior in which AI models pursue their goals through unintended or undesirable means. The company says it plans to share more details about this work in the future.
OpenAI has been scrambling in recent weeks to respond to what may be the most consequential safety incident in its history. Earlier this year, a set of rogue AI agents escaped internal testing sandboxes and breached the platform Hugging Face in a quest to complete a security evaluation. OpenAI failed to detect the agents’ behavior even as they spent weeks using a message board to coordinate their actions, raising questions about the company’s ability to monitor its models as they grow more powerful.
The saga prompted a reckoning inside OpenAI, forcing employees to consider whether there were lapses in its existing policies around safety, security, and alignment. Anthropic, Meta, and the Chinese AI startup Moonshoot have since disclosed similar incidents in which their AI agents escaped their sandboxes, indicating this is a broader problem facing AI companies.
OpenAI is now sharing more about its internal response to the growing cybercapabilities of its AI models, and said it plans to release a more detailed postmortem of the Hugging Face incident in the coming days. “Obviously, everything that we’re doing is intended to prevent something like Hugging Face from happening again,” said Glaese.
In a blog post published Tuesday, OpenAI says that immediately following the Hugging Face incident, it started working to secure its research environments. The company says it now requires stronger sandboxes for training its AI agents, and has implemented stricter controls to isolate them from the internet.
Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, told reporters that the company’s decision to strengthen its internal safeguards was triggered not only by what happened with Hugging Face, but also by two other recent events. One was an internal evaluation of Astra, which showed that the AI model performs significantly better on coding and cybersecurity tasks than its predecessors. The other was the general pace of AI progress that OpenAI is achieving internally, which Pachocki expects to continue.
“We really expect the pace of capability advancements to be quite a bit faster than in the past,” Pachocki said. “This led us to really focus on strengthening our safeguards.”
The rapid advances in the hacking capabilities of OpenAI’s latest models have prompted a swift response across the company. OpenAI president and cofounder Greg Brockman said in a blog post on Monday that the Hugging Face saga showed that the company had “underestimated the real-world cyber capabilities of our AI models.”

Landmark trial on Meta’s impact on children’s mental health begins in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:33:11 UTC
03:33:11 KST

Landmark trial on Meta’s impact on children’s mental health begins in US
Parent company for Facebook and Instagram is accused of deliberately designing its platforms to get children addicted.
Opening statements in a landmark case against Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, have begun in the United States, with California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey accusing the social media giant of deliberately making its platforms addictive to young people.
The trial, which is expected to last several weeks, began on Tuesday in a US federal court in California before District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. While there is an eight-person jury, the group is serving in an advisory role, as Judge Rogers will ultimately decide the case.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump’s approval rating sinks to new low at 33 percent
- list 2 of 4Canada battles the clock, politics in scramble to avert Trump’s tariffs
- list 3 of 4Disney sues US regulator, claiming political retaliation over ABC stations
- list 4 of 4Iran prepares to keep economy alive as US threatens further sanctions
Megan O’Neill, a deputy California attorney general, in her opening statement said that Meta designed its products to “hook the users, hold them for as long as they can, harvest their data, and then hide the truth from the public”.
She added that it worked “especially well for kids”.
California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were among the 29 states that sued the tech giant in 2023 over child safety and privacy. The other 25 will go to trial later.
The lawsuit accuses Meta of contributing to the youth mental health crisis by knowingly and deliberately designing features that addict children to its platforms and hiding these harms from the public. It also argues that Meta routinely collects data on children under 13 without their parents’ consent, in violation of federal law.
“Meta needed kids, and it needed to reassure the people who cared about those kids that the kids are safe,” O’Neill said.
The four states are seeking billions of dollars in damages as well as fundamental changes to how Meta runs its platforms.
‘Limited claims’
Meta has long pushed back on the allegations against it.
Meta’s lawyer Paul Schmidt told the court there was “no dispute” that some social media users face struggles, but that research showed no clear link between adolescents’ social media use and a lack of wellbeing.
He also said Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s cofounder and CEO, shared the company’s desire to improve its services, and not make them dangerous.
“They don’t believe they’re going to do well if people don’t like their service,” Schmidt said.
In a statement before the trial, a Meta spokesperson said the states’ claims are unsubstantiated, and the company stands by its record of creating strong protections for teenagers, including launching Instagram Teen Accounts in 2024, which limit who can contact underage users, as well as a feature that allows parents to set time limits on use.
If Judge Rogers finds Meta liable, she could impose civil penalties and order changes to Facebook and Instagram.
The potential impact on Meta’s bottom line is existential. The company could face fines as high as $1.4 trillion, which is just shy of its $1.5 trillion market cap. However, the coalition is seeking fines of roughly $200bn.
Meta has already been ordered to pay $942m in fines in a separate New Mexico lawsuit. These include $375m in civil penalties in a March jury verdict and $567m ordered by a judge earlier this month.
Meta has acknowledged that the lawsuits it faces, including those related to youth social media addiction, could lead to “substantial monetary damages or fines” in a US Securities and Exchange Commission filing in January.
Stephanie Otway, a Meta spokesperson, told Al Jazeera in a statement that while the state attorneys general call the trial “a landmark case”, their “limited claims are unsubstantiated and their financial demands are vastly disproportionate”.
She said the attorneys general offer “no proof anyone in their states was misled” and are attempting to “penalise Meta” for industry-wide challenges like age verification. “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout,” she added.
The first testimony
After opening arguments concluded, former Meta safety engineer Arturo Bejar began testifying as the states’ first witness. Bejar has long said Meta knew its child safety tools did not work, and has testified against the company in four trials.
Meta sought to block his testimony, allegedly for deleting Signal messages with former employees, but Rogers rejected what she considered a long-shot bid to eliminate a key witness.
Bejar told jurors that “move fast and break things” was a mantra at Meta, which took a “don’t ask, don’t tell” approach to monitoring whether children under 13 were online.
“Many products were shipped into the world”, such as Reels short-form videos, “and safety was not a consideration in how it was initially deployed”, Bejar said.
Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri are also expected to testify.
The trial is scheduled to last six weeks.
The case’s impetus came from a US Senate committee hearing in 2021, when whistleblower Frances Haugen, a former data scientist at Facebook, claimed the company knowingly pushed products that could impact the health of young users as it pursued higher profits.
Meta has repeatedly tried to end the coalition lawsuit, including in 2024, and as recently as June, when it sought summary judgement – a decision that a court might make without going to trial – which would have ended the lawsuit.
Al Jazeera’s Eva McKend, reporting from Washington, DC, said the states have a “substantial case”, but that “proving intent” will be their biggest challenge.
But, she said, “it speaks volumes that they were even able to get this far”. “No doubt, Meta, with all the corporate might that they have, have tried for a long time to get this squashed and not let this reach before a judge,” she added. “So [the company has] to be quite worried at this point.”
A long time coming
The case is affecting the company’s stock.
On Wall Street, Meta shares traded lower most of Tuesday and closed down 4.4 percent at $543.67.
The trial is the latest in an avalanche of lawsuits against Meta Platforms and other social media companies, including Google’s YouTube, TikTok and Snap, over arguments that their platforms harm young people, illegally collect their data and are deliberately designed to addict them.
As the trial began, child safety advocates and parents who trace their children’s deaths to social media harms gathered outside of the court on Tuesday. Many parents held photos of their late children as they spoke to reporters outside, at times through tears.
Several parents held a banner with the names and ages of children who died from social media-related harms. It was several feet long.
Among the people outside the court was Mary Rodee, who said her 15-year-old son Riley Basford died by suicide in 2021 after being victimised by a predator on Facebook.
“They call it spontaneous suicide,” she said. “I call it what it was: the predictable outcome of a system that protects corporations instead of children.”
