News Analysis: How "Nanjing Massacre" was distorted into "Nanjing Incident" at Nagasaki A-bomb museum
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
19:06:33 CST
20:06:33 KST

TOKYO, Aug. 18 (Xinhua) -- The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum is one of the few public facilities in Japan that still uses the term "Nanjing Massacre" in its exhibit descriptions.
However, the new exhibition text unveiled by the museum on July 28 shows that starting in March next year, references to the "Nanjing Massacre" will be changed to the "Nanjing Incident."
The Nagasaki municipal government, which oversees the museum, claimed that the revision was intended to "align" the wording with official Japanese terminology and mainstream textbooks.
The Nanjing Massacre, backed by overwhelming evidence, is a horrendous crime committed by Japanese militarists that admits no distortion or denial. The Tokyo Trials ruled in black and white that the wartime atrocities of the Japanese army in Nanjing constituted a "massacre," not a mere "incident."
Many Japanese observers therefore see the move as another step backward in Japan's reckoning with its wartime past.
DECADES-LONG DISPUTE OVER EXHIBITS
The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum stands about 150 meters southeast of the atomic bomb hypocenter. In its third exhibition hall, a large timeline titled "The Sino-Japanese War and the Pacific War" chronicles the historical arc from 1931 to 1945.
Under the entry for 1937, it reads: "December: Nanjing was occupied; a massacre occurred," accompanied by a photograph of Japanese troops checking Chinese civilians fleeing the war.
Behind the exhibits lies a decades-long dispute over how history should be presented at the museum. Noboru Sakiyama, 67, chairman of the Nagasaki Museum for Human Rights and Peace, knows the ins and outs all too well.
The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum opened in April 1996, but the dispute over the content of its exhibits had already begun before then.
According to Sakiyama, the museum originally planned to display historical photographs related to the Nanjing Massacre, Unit 731, and the Japanese military's wartime "comfort women" system.
Before the museum opened, however, the Nagasaki municipal government, under pressure from conservative lawmakers and right-wing groups, announced that a photograph of the Nanjing Massacre would be replaced with one showing Japanese troops "entering Nanjing."
That change sparked strong opposition from progressive groups, prompting the museum to replace the photograph with a still image taken from video footage showing Japanese soldiers driving Nanjing residents toward massacre sites.
The backlash from Japan's right-wing forces intensified in the month the museum opened. Over a hundred sound trucks were mobilized to stage protests around Nagasaki city hall and the atomic bomb museum. An organization calling itself the "citizens' association to correct the Nagasaki atomic bomb exhibits," founded that same year, even filed a lawsuit against the museum.
Under mounting pressure, the Nagasaki municipal government announced that year that it would remove the relevant photographs, text and video materials from the museum.
The Japanese right-wing forces did not let up in the years that followed, and their campaigns only grew more aggressive.
In October 2020, Masamitsu Watanabe, head of the aforementioned group for correcting atomic bomb exhibits, visited the museum and demanded that it revise the references to the "Nanjing Massacre" in its exhibits. The group also repeatedly urged conservative lawmakers to pressure the Nagasaki municipal government.
In response, 20 organizations, including the Nagasaki Museum for Human Rights and Peace, formed the "Nagasaki citizens' association for atomic bomb exhibits to be shared with the world," calling on the city to maintain the term "Nanjing Massacre" in the exhibits.
Sakiyama still remembers the words of former Nagasaki Mayor Iccho Itoh: "Nagasaki has always called internationally for building a world free of nuclear weapons, but without our own reflection, appeals for the abolition of nuclear weapons will never reach the world."
AN ABSURD "CITIZEN'S LETTER"
Last year brought a major shift in the decades-long dispute surrounding the Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum.
In the fall of 2025, the municipal government gave an interim report to the museum's operation council on the detailed plan for renewing the exhibits, proposing to change the description of "Nanjing was occupied; a massacre occurred" to "The Nanjing Incident, in which large numbers of civilians and prisoners of war were killed."
The change immediately drew opposition from numerous progressive groups. At a meeting of the museum's operation council this February, a representative of a Japanese civic group bluntly pointed out that exhibits downplaying Japan's history as an aggressor would be difficult for the international community to accept.
Yet on the local government's website, a comment on the museum's exhibits steeped in historical revisionism was selected for publication in the citizens' opinions and suggestions section.
The "suggestion" raised a string of absurd claims, such as demanding the museum to "immediately end the display of the Nanjing Incident, since there is no evidence for it," asserting that "the Nanjing Incident is clearly propaganda by the Chinese or U.S. governments," and arguing that "many foreigner and students visit the museum, and the museum must stop disseminating false history."
In response to the opinion, the relevant division of the Nagasaki municipal government said the description "Nanjing was occupied; a massacre occurred" would, in the exhibit renewal, reference the wording used in junior high and high school history textbooks approved by Japan's education ministry.
More tellingly, Watanabe, who has long pressured the museum to change how it describes the "Nanjing Massacre," participated in discussions on the exhibit renewal plan as a member of the museum's operation council.
Takakage Fujita, secretary-general of the Association for Inheriting and Propagating the Murayama Statement, said that for various reasons, right-wing forces are infiltrating the museum's operation council.
He noted that the Nanjing Massacre was one of the most brutal crimes committed by Japan in its modern history and stands as an emblematic event demonstrating the nature of Japan's war of aggression.
Eighty-one years after the end of the war, Nagasaki is taking advantage of the museum's exhibit renewal to replace the historical description of "massacre" with the term "Nanjing Incident," which denies the aggressive nature of the brutal act, Fujita said, adding that such a move is unacceptable under any circumstances.
HISTORY OF AGGRESSION MUST NOT BE ERASED
In March this year, Nagasaki City finalized the plan for updating exhibits at the atomic bomb museum. The third exhibition hall will see the most sweeping changes: the wall-length timeline titled "The Sino-Japanese War and the Pacific War" will be removed altogether, replaced by exhibits on the two World Wars.
The change troubles Sakiyama deeply. "We have called for the timeline to be kept, as well as the video section, where footage gives a clear and direct sense of Japan's history of aggression. But they plan to turn that area into a lounge," he said.
The current timeline makes several references to Japan's invasion of China. In 1937, multiple entries read: "July: The Lugou Bridge Incident; war with China begins," "August: Naval aircraft took off from Omura Airport, crossed the sea and bombed Nanjing," and "December: Nanjing was occupied; a massacre occurred."
"Without the wartime timeline, young Japanese visitors will struggle to grasp the full picture of history," Sakiyama said. "These events were originally laid out clearly in the timeline. It is difficult to convey such an overarching historical context through individual exhibit panels."
The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum has been one of the few public institutions in Japan still using the term "Nanjing Massacre." Sakiyama is deeply concerned that the museum is now set to give ground as well.
In his view, the change reflects a political trend that has continued since the 2015 "Abe Statement" and has been further intensified under the administration of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi -- an attempt "to wipe out Japan's history of aggression in past wars."
Sakiyama said many ordinary Japanese people, particularly the younger generation, view Japan as a victim of the war, especially because of the atomic bombings.
He said messages left by young visitors at the Nagasaki Museum for Human Rights and Peace show that many young Japanese people only learned about Japan's aggression against other Asian countries and regions after visiting the museum.
Even visitors who had some knowledge of that history, Sakiyama added, only came to grasp the full extent of the atrocities committed by Japanese militarists after visiting the museum.
"Japanese people know very little about their own country's history of aggression," Sakiyama said. "Unless we face the historical facts squarely, reflect on them deeply, and hold firm to the commitment never to repeat the mistakes of war, Japan will be unable to build genuine friendship and trust with other countries. In that case, the so-called 'peaceful homeland' will be nothing more than empty talk." ■

Analysts see NEEAP 2.0 to accelerate Malaysia energy efficiency push
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
19:06:03 CST
20:06:03 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Aug. 18 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's recently launched National Energy Efficiency Policy and Action Plan 2026-2035 (NEEAP 2.0) is expected to accelerate the adoption of energy-efficiency measures across industries, commercial buildings and households, with analysts seeing stronger opportunities for energy-efficiency solution providers as regulatory enforcement gains traction.
MBSB Research said in a recent note that NEEAP 2.0, together with the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Act, creates a regulatory framework to systematically reduce energy consumption across factories, buildings and households.
Malaysia launched NEEAP 2.0 last week as part of its broader energy transition, shifting greater emphasis towards improving energy efficiency alongside expanding energy supply. The plan targets an 11.6 percent reduction in energy demand by 2035, underpinned by an estimated 36.6 billion ringgit (about 9.02 billion U.S. dollars) in investment across industrial, commercial and domestic users.
MBSB Research said about 9.1 billion ringgit of the estimated investment could be concentrated in industrial and commercial private-sector opportunities, spanning industrial utilities, high-efficiency motors, automation, heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) and chillers, heat recovery, mechanical and electrical (M&E) retrofits and district cooling.
The much larger 26.9 billion ringgit domestic component is expected to be driven mainly by the adoption and replacement of household appliances with higher-efficiency models, which MBSB Research viewed as largely voluntary.
Kenanga Research also described NEEAP 2.0 as a structural catalyst for energy-efficiency adoption, with EECA enforcement expected to gradually shift spending towards compliance-driven investments.
While data centers are currently excluded from the specific commercial-building energy-audit program under NEEAP 2.0, it expects their high energy intensity to continue driving demand for integrated facilities and energy-management solutions, with scope for tighter efficiency requirements over time.
Hong Leong Investment Research also said that NEEAP 2.0 offered an attractive 2.33 times benefit-cost ratio, meaning projected energy-cost savings would exceed the investment cost. ■

Taiwan launches first live-fire exercise with first-person view drones
The island’s military is working to learn the lessons of the Ukraine war and boost its asymmetric defences against the PLA
Taiwan’s army has for the first time used first-person view (FPV) drones against armoured vehicles in a live-fire exercise, adopting tactics pioneered during the Ukraine war to strengthen its asymmetric capabilities against the People’s Liberation Army.
The exercise on Monday highlighted efforts to broaden strike options beyond traditional firepower such as rocket systems and heavy artillery.
The Army Unmanned Systems Training Command brought together six units from the military’s artillery commands, Marine Corps and Military Police for the exercise.
Under simulated battlefield conditions, operators flew FPV drones carrying armour-piercing warheads against decommissioned tanks and armoured ammunition carriers.
FPV drones – which stream real-time video directly to a pair of goggles worn by the pilot – are usually designed to be more manoeuvrable and acrobatic than other drones, allowing greater accuracy in combat.
The drones conducted frontal and flanking strikes in both single-drone and coordinated two-drone attacks, according to the Youth Daily News, a defence ministry-affiliated newspaper based in Taipei.

Taiwan says its commitment to strengthening economic and trade ties with Lithuania remains unchanged as the two sides resume negotiations on an economic cooperation action plan.
“Our determination to work alongside the new Lithuanian government to strengthen economic and trade cooperation remains unchanged,” Eric Huang, director general of the Department of European Affairs at Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said Tuesday.
The negotiations were briefly suspended in June as Lithuania’s Social Democrats reshuffled the Cabinet and resumed in late July.
Huang said details of the action plan were still being finalised, with the two sides maintaining close contact over the planned cooperation.
Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry has not disclosed specific details of the plan, citing ongoing consultations. It said the focus was on “building sustainable economic ties that would contribute to the development of the country’s high-tech sectors”.
Expectations for closer economic ties with Taiwan grew in 2021 after Taiwan opened its representative office in Vilnius. But Lithuanian officials have more recently expressed frustration over what they consider insufficient Taiwanese investment in Lithuania.
The opening of the office triggered a diplomatic dispute between Lithuania and China. Beijing viewed the decision to use “Taiwanese” rather than “Taipei” in the office’s name as support for Taiwan’s efforts to establish itself as an independent state. Taiwan maintains representative offices under the name Taipei in many other countries.
Huang’s comments came after US lawmakers urged Lithuanian leaders to continue their “bold path” of maintaining ties with Taipei and not give in to pressure from Beijing.
At the same time, Lithuania’s ruling coalition has increasingly discussed normalising relations with China. The government’s program calls for restoring diplomatic representation with Beijing to levels comparable with those maintained by other European Union member states.
Lithuania established closer ties with Taiwan under a previous conservative-led government, prompting a sharp deterioration in relations with China. The issue has since remained politically sensitive in Vilnius as successive governments have sought to balance economic interests, relations with Beijing and support for Taiwan.

====================================================================================================

Medicinal mushroom supplements linked to a sudden relapse of psychosis in new case report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
11:00:23 UTC
20:00:23 KST

A recent medical report details the case of a young man whose psychotic symptoms worsened sharply after he took non-prescription medicinal mushroom supplements. Published in the Primary Care Companion for CNS Disorders, the paper suggests that seemingly harmless natural remedies might carry unexpected psychiatric risks for certain individuals. The observations highlight the necessity of discussing all dietary supplements with a doctor, especially when managing complex mental health conditions.
Dietary supplements, including vitamins, herbs, and mushroom extracts, are incredibly popular for their perceived health benefits. Many people assume that because these products are natural, they are entirely safe to consume. A growing body of medical literature indicates that various natural ingredients can sometimes trigger psychiatric issues or interact poorly with standard medications. Past research provides evidence of severe anxiety, confusion, and even hallucinations linked to certain plant-based pills and herbal extracts.
Psychiatrists Kirat Kaur and Shobit Garg authored the new case report to draw attention to these overlooked risks. Their work builds on earlier medical records documenting similar unusual reactions to over-the-counter remedies. A 2016 medical report described a man who developed severe paranoia and hallucinations after taking multiple brain support supplements and weight loss pills. Once the man stopped taking the supplements, his psychological symptoms faded, suggesting a link between the herbal ingredients and his mental distress.
The active ingredients in many natural products can sometimes alter the way the brain processes dopamine and serotonin. These are neurotransmitters, which are chemical messengers that help regulate mood, thoughts, and perception. When these chemicals become unbalanced, it can lead to perceptual disturbances like seeing or hearing things that are not there. Some plant extracts can also inhibit enzymes in the digestive system, changing how the body absorbs and processes conventional medications.
Because the dietary supplement industry lacks rigorous government oversight, products can contain unlisted ingredients or varying concentrations of active compounds. Historical reviews of herbal medicine have shown that poorly regulated products sometimes contain hidden prescription drugs or heavy metals. Even without contamination, natural neuroactive compounds can place stress on a vulnerable nervous system. Decades of traditional use in various cultures do not always guarantee modern safety, especially for people with complicated medical histories.
In the recent report, Kaur and Garg detail the experience of a 24-year-old man from India. The patient had a history of cerebral palsy, a group of disorders affecting movement and muscle tone, caused by a brain injury around the time of his birth. He also had a mild intellectual disability and relied on caregivers for his daily activities. He had no previous history of psychiatric illness or substance abuse.
The man was brought to a psychiatric clinic after developing distressing auditory hallucinations over a two-month period. He described hearing a female voice that criticized his actions and made derogatory comments. These hallucinations occurred multiple times a day and caused him intense anxiety and agitation. He did not experience any visual hallucinations or delusional beliefs.
To treat the symptoms, doctors prescribed risperidone, an antipsychotic medication commonly used to manage schizophrenia and related disorders. They also prescribed etizolam to reduce his anxiety and propranolol to control his physical stress responses. Within a few days of starting this medication regimen, his hallucinations faded in intensity, and his overall behavior improved.
After he showed this initial improvement, his family decided to give him a dietary supplement without consulting his doctors. The product was a mushroom-based blend marketed to boost immune function and cognitive health. It contained high doses of extracts from several mushrooms, including lion’s mane, shiitake, reishi, and turkey tail. The family gave him a daily dose of roughly 1,280 milligrams of these combined mushroom extracts.
Within two to three days of starting the supplement, the man experienced a drastic return of his psychotic symptoms. The auditory hallucinations became much more frequent and intense, and he grew highly fearful and agitated. His prescribed psychiatric medications had not been changed in any way. The doctors suspected the newly introduced mushroom blend was responsible for the sudden decline in his mental state.
Recognizing the timeline of events, the family immediately stopped giving him the supplement. Over the next few days, his severe symptoms faded, and he returned to the stable state he had achieved before taking the mushrooms. This rapid recovery after removing the product provides evidence linking the mushroom extract to the sudden relapse. The doctors continued his standard psychiatric medications without any further issues.
Kaur and Garg suggest that medicinal mushrooms like lion’s mane might alter brain chemistry in unintended ways. These mushrooms are known to promote nerve growth factors, which are proteins that help maintain and grow brain cells. This process might inadvertently shift the balance of neurotransmitters in the brain. For someone with a preexisting brain injury like cerebral palsy, this shift might disrupt a fragile neurological system and trigger psychotic symptoms.
Medical case reports focus on the experiences of a single individual, making it difficult to generalize the findings to the broader population. A single observation cannot establish a direct cause and effect relationship between an ingredient and a symptom. The man’s reaction might have been an uncommon response due to his specific medical history, his existing medications, or an unlisted contaminant in the supplement itself. This specific case does not indicate that non-hallucinogenic mushroom supplements pose a severe psychiatric threat to healthy individuals.
Individual medical cases help doctors identify potential rare side effects that large clinical trials might miss. They offer early warnings for medical professionals to monitor in other patients, particularly those with underlying vulnerabilities. Scientists need to conduct larger, controlled studies to understand how medicinal mushrooms interact with brain chemistry and psychiatric medications. Until then, the report indicates that doctors should routinely ask their patients about any non-prescription products they might be taking.
The report, “Exacerbation of Psychotic Symptoms Associated With Mushroom-Based Supplementation in a Patient With Cerebral Palsy,” was authored by Kirat Kaur and Shobit Garg.

Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles (L) shakes hands with Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi during a press conference at Parliament House in Canberra. (AFP photo)
Japan underlined on Aug. 18 the “critical” importance of security cooperation with the United States and South Korea, after President Donald Trump alarmed allies by scaling back military drills with Seoul while hailing his ties with Pyongyang.
Trump abruptly announced on Aug. 16 that he had ordered the Pentagon to scale back “inappropriate and hostile” military drills with South Korea, a day before the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises got underway.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, on a visit to Australia, supported security cooperation with key defense backer Washington and neighbor Seoul.
“As Japan faces the most severe and complicated security environment in the post-war era, the cooperation among Japan, the United States and South Korea is critical to the peace and stability of the region,” Koizumi told journalists.

Pressed about whether Kim had responded to his messages, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office: “Yeah, he has.”

Seoul’s unification ministry, responsible for relations with the North, said it “cannot verify the specific content of the exchanges” between Washington and Pyongyang.

South Korean officials have said the exercises had begun as planned and that they hoped the personal chemistry between Trump and Kim would bring them back to talks.
Seoul’s Presidential Office said on Aug. 18 that the drills did not reflect “any intention to attack North Korea or escalate tensions on the Korean peninsula.”
North Korea has not responded publicly, although it has previously voiced anger at the regular joint maneuvers that take place in the South.
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles, hosting his Japanese counterpart, said Canberra was “very concerned about North Korea’s nuclear program as well as its missile program.”
Trump again called into question on Aug. 17 U.S. support for both South Korea and NATO allies that have refused to contribute to the Iran war.
“We have 39,000 soldiers over there, guarding you from Kim Jong Un, your next-door neighbor, and you’re not going to help us on a very easy military operation in Iran. That’s strange,” Trump said in the Oval Office, giving a deployment figure that exceeds official troop numbers.
Seoul said on Aug. 18 that it had been involved in consultations with the United States and other partners over freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and possible military contributions.

Israeli flags raise questions over Israel's plans in Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
10:56:25 UTC
19:56:25 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli flags on southern Lebanon highway fuel fears of permanent occupation
Israeli flags planted along a main road inside southern Lebanon have fuelled anger and renewed questions over whether Israel's expanding military presence is becoming an open-ended occupation, as its forces intensify bombardments, demolitions and earthworks across the south.
The flags were seen flying along the Naqoura-Tyre coastal road, one of southern Lebanon's main arteries and a route regularly used by UN peacekeepers.
Footage published by Israeli Channel 12 journalist Amit Segal appeared to have been filmed from an Israeli military vehicle, while Segal said the video had been sent to him by Israeli soldiers.
UNIFIL confirmed that its peacekeepers had observed several Israeli flags on Lebanese territory, including along the coastal road and in the village of Naqoura, and said their presence constituted a violation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
The images have taken on added significance as Israel entrenches itself across parts of southern Lebanon, where it established an alleged "security zone" after invading a swathe of the country during its latest war on Lebanon.
Israel claims the zone is necessary to protect its northern communities from Hezbollah. But the raising of Israeli flags on Lebanese soil, alongside continuing military construction, demolitions and Israeli declarations that its troops will remain until Hezbollah is disarmed, has heightened concerns that what Israel may claim to be a temporary security arrangement is taking on the characteristics of a prolonged occupation.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said last week that Israeli forces would not withdraw from southern Lebanon until Hezbollah had been disarmed. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has presented the buffer zone as one of Israel's military achievements.
Israel's military rejected suggestions that its presence was directed against Lebanon itself.
"Israel is not acting against the Lebanese state or its citizens," the military said, maintaining that its forces were operating in southern Lebanon to remove threats posed by Hezbollah.
That claim has increasingly been challenged by developments on the ground, where Israeli operations have struck civilian areas and infrastructure.
Like in Judea and Samaria: Israeli flags are flying along Lebanon’s coastal road, between Naqoura and Tyre. pic.twitter.com/rym6rwNKXD
— Amit Segal (@AmitSegal) August 16, 2026
Israeli forces dynamite water reservoir
On Tuesday, Israeli forces dynamited a water reservoir on municipal land in Mansouri, in the Tyre district, which supplied the village with water, according to L'Orient-Le Jour's correspondent in southern Lebanon.
Israeli artillery repeatedly shelled Mansouri at around 11 am, before targeting the outskirts of Mayfadoun and Zawtar al-Sharqiyah in the Nabatieh district.
Israeli bulldozers were also carrying out earthworks on Mansouri's municipal lands, while Israeli soldiers opened machine-gun fire towards Haddatha in the Bint Jbeil district. At least one building was dynamited on the outskirts of Shebaa, near Birket al-Naqqar.
Earlier on Tuesday, witnesses reported seeing an Israeli bulldozer clearing land near Birket al-Naqqar, while two Merkava tanks took up positions in the area.
The attacks on Mansouri began before dawn and continued through the morning.
Two three-storey buildings were destroyed in an early-morning attack on the village, while shortly before 9 am Israeli shelling was continuing and a Merkava tank was firing towards the centre of the village. Machine-gun fire also swept through the area, witnesses said.
Residents reported hearing tanks advancing towards state-owned land in Mansouri and seeing a house on fire.
Between 2 am and 4 am, Israeli aircraft also bombed the outskirts of Deir Siriane and residential areas of Mansouri, while artillery struck Dohat Kfar Remmane and the Ali Taher hills in Nabatieh.
At least 10 towns and villages were bombarded by Israel on Monday alone, while significant demolition operations targeted homes and infrastructure in four southern Lebanese localities.
UN records 137 Israeli projectiles a day
The latest operations a significant increase in Israeli military activity in southern Lebanon.
UNIFIL said it recorded an average of 137 projectiles a day between 5 and 16 August, including 208 on Saturday and 185 on Sunday.
The UN force said civilians were once again bearing the brunt of the escalation, with families forced to leave their homes or change their daily lives because of insecurity and uncertainty.
Peacekeepers have continued patrols, monitoring developments, clearing roads, reducing explosive hazards and facilitating humanitarian access, the force said.
UNIFIL reiterated that Resolution 1701 remained the central framework for restoring stability and called for renewed adherence to its provisions.
A US-brokered arrangement envisages a progressive Israeli withdrawal linked to the verified disarmament of Hezbollah. Hezbollah, however, has rejected discussions over its weapons before Israeli forces withdraw from Lebanese territory.
Since Israel launched its war on Lebanon in March, almost 4,400 people have been killed and over 12,300 injuried.

Israeli flags on southern Lebanon highway fuel fears of permanent occupation
Israeli flags planted along a main road inside southern Lebanon have fuelled anger and renewed questions over whether Israel's expanding military presence is becoming an open-ended occupation, as its forces intensify bombardments, demolitions and earthworks across the south.
The flags were seen flying along the Naqoura-Tyre coastal road, one of southern Lebanon's main arteries and a route regularly used by UN peacekeepers.
Footage published by Israeli Channel 12 journalist Amit Segal appeared to have been filmed from an Israeli military vehicle, while Segal said the video had been sent to him by Israeli soldiers.
UNIFIL confirmed that its peacekeepers had observed several Israeli flags on Lebanese territory, including along the coastal road and in the village of Naqoura, and said their presence constituted a violation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
The images have taken on added significance as Israel entrenches itself across parts of southern Lebanon, where it established an alleged "security zone" after invading a swathe of the country during its latest war on Lebanon.
Israel claims the zone is necessary to protect its northern communities from Hezbollah. But the raising of Israeli flags on Lebanese soil, alongside continuing military construction, demolitions and Israeli declarations that its troops will remain until Hezbollah is disarmed, has heightened concerns that what Israel may claim to be a temporary security arrangement is taking on the characteristics of a prolonged occupation.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said last week that Israeli forces would not withdraw from southern Lebanon until Hezbollah had been disarmed. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has presented the buffer zone as one of Israel's military achievements.
Israel's military rejected suggestions that its presence was directed against Lebanon itself.
"Israel is not acting against the Lebanese state or its citizens," the military said, maintaining that its forces were operating in southern Lebanon to remove threats posed by Hezbollah.
That claim has increasingly been challenged by developments on the ground, where Israeli operations have struck civilian areas and infrastructure.

Israeli forces dynamite water reservoir
On Tuesday, Israeli forces dynamited a water reservoir on municipal land in Mansouri, in the Tyre district, which supplied the village with water, according to L'Orient-Le Jour's correspondent in southern Lebanon.
Israeli artillery repeatedly shelled Mansouri at around 11 am, before targeting the outskirts of Mayfadoun and Zawtar al-Sharqiyah in the Nabatieh district.
Israeli bulldozers were also carrying out earthworks on Mansouri's municipal lands, while Israeli soldiers opened machine-gun fire towards Haddatha in the Bint Jbeil district. At least one building was dynamited on the outskirts of Shebaa, near Birket al-Naqqar.
Earlier on Tuesday, witnesses reported seeing an Israeli bulldozer clearing land near Birket al-Naqqar, while two Merkava tanks took up positions in the area.
The attacks on Mansouri began before dawn and continued through the morning.
Two three-storey buildings were destroyed in an early-morning attack on the village, while shortly before 9 am Israeli shelling was continuing and a Merkava tank was firing towards the centre of the village. Machine-gun fire also swept through the area, witnesses said.
Residents reported hearing tanks advancing towards state-owned land in Mansouri and seeing a house on fire.
Between 2 am and 4 am, Israeli aircraft also bombed the outskirts of Deir Siriane and residential areas of Mansouri, while artillery struck Dohat Kfar Remmane and the Ali Taher hills in Nabatieh.
At least 10 towns and villages were bombarded by Israel on Monday alone, while significant demolition operations targeted homes and infrastructure in four southern Lebanese localities.
UN records 137 Israeli projectiles a day
The latest operations a significant increase in Israeli military activity in southern Lebanon.
UNIFIL said it recorded an average of 137 projectiles a day between 5 and 16 August, including 208 on Saturday and 185 on Sunday.
The UN force said civilians were once again bearing the brunt of the escalation, with families forced to leave their homes or change their daily lives because of insecurity and uncertainty.
Peacekeepers have continued patrols, monitoring developments, clearing roads, reducing explosive hazards and facilitating humanitarian access, the force said.
UNIFIL reiterated that Resolution 1701 remained the central framework for restoring stability and called for renewed adherence to its provisions.
A US-brokered arrangement envisages a progressive Israeli withdrawal linked to the verified disarmament of Hezbollah. Hezbollah, however, has rejected discussions over its weapons before Israeli forces withdraw from Lebanese territory.
Since Israel launched its war on Lebanon in March, almost 4,400 people have been killed and over 12,300 injuried.

‘Migration has been weaponised’: Italy’s security law criticised after death of Moroccan man in police restraint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
10:55:44 UTC
19:55:44 KST

If, before 19 July, few people in Italy beyond his family and friends knew who Abderrahim Fakir was, by the late afternoon of that day the final moments of his life were being watched across the country.
Video footage widely shared online showed him being handcuffed and forcibly restrained by police on a street in Pilastro, a neighbourhood in the north-east of Bologna.
Fakir, a 42-year-old small business owner born in Morocco but who had lived in Italy since he was a child, was pinned to the ground by two police officers as emergency health workers looked on. He repeatedly begged for help before his body stopped moving.
Fakir was pronounced dead at the scene. The cause of death is still being established, although an initial postmortem indicated lung compression.
Outrage over Fakir’s death spilled well beyond Pilastro, prompting protests in Bologna and Rome and fuelling a tense national debate over the far-right government’s approach to policing and immigration. It also put a wide-ranging security bill enacted by Giorgia Meloni’s ruling coalition under renewed scrutiny.
Fakir’s is the first case in which a new legal shield giving public officials greater protection from prosecution if it can be demonstrated they acted in self-defence or within the line of duty, has been invoked.
As a result, although prosecutors in Bologna are investigating the two officers and four healthcare workers in connection to an inquiry into involuntary manslaughter, they will not be formally registered as criminal suspects unless authorities determine the use of restraint was unjustified.
The legal team for the two officers – who returned to work on Monday – strongly deny excessive force was used, maintaining they fully complied with official protocol. Lawyers for the healthcare workers, meanwhile, said they acted in strict accordance with emergency medical guidelines.
Critics of the legal shield have condemned the measure as giving too much power to the police, making it harder to hold them accountable.
Fabio Anselmo, the Fakir family lawyer, claimed it potentially risked “sabotaging” the investigation. “In this case, this is a rule that could effectively create impunity,” he said.
In Pilastro, a working-class neighbourhood with a population of about 7,000, of whom 25% are immigrants, family and friends of Fakir are also worried that politics will tamper with justice.
A banner tied to railings on the corner of Via Italo Svevo, the street where he died, reads: “Truth and justice for Fakir – the state kills.” Similar messages are scrawled on bus stops.
Fakir lived in another area of Bologna but often returned to Pilastro to see his brother, Mohamed, and friends from his childhood, including fellow Moroccan national Mike El Canas.
El Canas said Fakir was with a group of friends, who described him as being in good spirits, on the night before his death and stayed in Pilastro overnight.
“He was a good person, so kind and full of life,” said El Canas. “He had plenty of friends among the Moroccan community, but also Italians.”
It is unclear what happened in the hours before he died.
Police said they responded to concerns from residents about a man behaving erratically and aggressively. They called the health services, telling staff he was “having a psychiatric episode”. Other videos filmed by residents before police intervened showed Fakir in a state of extreme agitation and confusion. It later emerged he had been referred for mental health treatment in June.
In a letter published by La Repubblica, Barbara Spinelli, a lawyer who was assisting Fakir in renewing his residence permit, wrote that he feared being deported owing to the EU’s “return hubs” migration pact, despite her reassurances, and felt sorry about having to lay people off because of a slowdown in business.
Speaking to the Guardian from Casablanca, where family members in Italy had travelled to be with relatives as they await the repatriation of his body for burial alongside his late mother, Fakir’s sister Khadija said he had confided in her about relationship difficulties, but was otherwise always thinking of others.
Exacerbating the family’s grief is the way in which some far-right politicians and factions of Italy’s rightwing press dehumanised Fakir, seizing on drugs convictions in his youth and portraying him as just another immigrant causing trouble.
“Abderrahim helped those in need and was friendly and joked with everyone. This was Abderrahim,” said Khadija.
Khadija said she couldn’t bring herself to watch the videos but a witness told her Fakir was agitated and asking for help. “They could have calmed him down with something. Why did he have to end up in the hands of the police like that?”
After setting up a crowdfunding page to help cover legal costs, she said her family was hit with a deluge of online comments accusing them of trying to make money. “I would pay €3m to have my brother back,” she said. “All we want is truth and justice from the Italian state. Whoever acted wrongfully must pay.”
People living in Pilastro are familiar with being disparaged. The neighbourhood came under the political spotlight during a regional election campaign in early 2020 when Matteo Salvini, the leader of the far-right League and the current deputy prime minister, rang the bell of a Tunisian family’s home to ask them over the intercom if they were drug dealers. Salvini, who in the past has posed in police uniform, has defended the police over Fakir’s death.
Pilastro has also felt the brunt of a measure in the security bill cracking down on peaceful dissent after 33 people racked up thousands of euros in fines between them during a protest earlier this year against the construction of a museum that would swallow up a significant portion of the area’s only park. One person was detained for a couple of days for climbing a tree.
However, many are too afraid to speak out, even more so after Fakir’s death. “The police have the power, a uniform that protects them, and we are nobodies,” said El Canas. “But we must speak up, as otherwise, where will us ordinary citizens end up?”
Anselmo said that while the majority of Italy’s police officers were good, there were those who “inevitably absorb the political climate in which they operate”.
With Meloni striving to secure a second mandate in next year’s general election, while fending off a new far-right rival, Roberto Vannacci, the climate is only expected to become more divisive as she promotes her main political offerings – security and immigration, with the latter evident in her response to the mass migrant crossing from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.
“The Fakir story illustrates how words and these kinds of bills actually play out on the ground,” said Cecilia Sottilotta, an associate politics professor at the Università per Stranieri in Perugia. “But these security measures have long been in the plans of Italy’s far right, who have always insisted that the police should have a free rein. Now, the big picture is very important. Migration has been weaponised. Again, this is not new, but we will see more of it with elections coming up.”

Waiting for zero hour: A countdown to war in Yemen?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
10:55:12 UTC
19:55:12 KST

Breadcrumb
Waiting for zero hour: A countdown to war in Yemen?
Since early August, the Houthis, officially known as the Ansar Allah movement, have launched drone and ballistic missile attacks across several governorates under the control of Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.
The deadly attacks have heavily targeted the city of Mocha in the Taiz governorate and Marib in the eastern part of the country, and fighting has broken out in border areas between the Houthis and Yemen's government forces.
Dozens of people have been killed or injured as a result of this escalation, which first reignited in mid-July when Yemeni government forces bombed the runway of Houthi-controlled Sanaa airport after an Iranian aircraft landed, violating an agreement between Yemen's warring parties which had kept the civil war relatively dormant since 2022.
Since then, the Houthis have systematically targeted Saudi-linked ships in the Red Sea, while also expanding their attacks to Yemeni infrastructure.
Last week, the group fired missiles at a Yemeni-owned ship near Mocha, killing four crew members. Attacks on the Red Sea port city have left at least 16 dead and 22 injured in August alone, according to the port’s manager.
The Yemeni government has responded to these attacks with retaliatory strikes of its own, according to military spokesperson Colonel Majed Al-Nuzaili.
On Sunday, he announced that the Yemeni Armed Forces had carried out over 180 military operations targeting Houthi weapon depots and military equipment. According to military sources cited in the Yemeni media, over 200 Houthi fighters were killed in 48 hours, most in the southwestern Taiz province.
In response, the Houthis reportedly freed over 850 prisoners in Saada, Hajjah, and Sanaa in exchange for joining their ranks in combat.
In addition to domestic attacks, the group has also targeted Saudi Arabia’s Aramco refinery in Jazan, attacking the Red Sea facility with drones for the second time on Thursday.
Political analysts told The New Arab that the Houthis are launching offensives in government-held territories to pressure both the internationally recognised government and Saudi Arabia into granting key political concessions.
These include resuming public sector salary payments and fully lifting restrictions on Sanaa Airport.
However, for the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), the executive body of Yemen's internationally recognised government, any large-scale response is riddled with complex strategic considerations.
An inevitable return to war?
Professor Abdulsattar Al-Shamiri, a Yemeni political analyst and CEO of Johood Centre for Studies and Research, told The New Arab that the Houthis are applying intense pressure at a time in which the government is refraining from engaging in a full-scale confrontation “out of caution”.
"They must consider that a new open battle could prove far more destructive to infrastructure and civilians than the earlier rounds in 2015 and 2016,” he said.
During both those periods of fighting, an estimated 30,000 people were killed, with millions of Yemenis left in poverty.
The caution of government forces, however, could wane if the conflict between the US and Iran de-escalates.
Professor Islam Al Mansi, an Egyptian political analyst based in Cairo, termed the PLC's calculations as “protective”, with a desire to avoid dragging Yemen back to all-out civil war or reviving a devastating cycle of internal conflict.
“The Houthis are unconcerned with such calculations because they act on external orders and execute a foreign Iranian agenda, completely detached from these considerations,” Al Mansi told The New Arab.
Furthering that point, Professor Mansour Al Mantaser, a Yemeni political analyst and former professor at Sanaa University, argued that the PLC's current stalling of a decisive military confrontation is linked to the Houthis’ role as Iran's proxy, which requires operating in ways that avoid directly dragging Tehran in.
“Iran benefits from maintaining a Houthi stronghold, and various parties use this conflict to advance their own interests without any regard for the Yemeni people,” he told The New Arab.
Asked whether a return to full-blown war is inevitable for Yemen, Al Shamiri said that “ultimately, the legitimate government will find itself forced into a comprehensive confrontation, particularly along the fronts of Hodeidah, Mocha, and Al-Barh”.
The Yemeni government has recognised that a military solution is “its only option,” Al Mansi said. Any preparations for “zero hour”, however, remain “tied to specific developments and strategic calculations”.
This caution from the PLC is connected to the government's relative lack of autonomy in its position within the broader Saudi-led coalition, describing their status quo as de facto “paralysis”.
“Even when opportunities arise, and regional or international actors need the Yemeni government to take the initiative, it unfortunately fails to seize these moments under the pretext of 'fully preparing for the battle',” Al Mantaser told The New Arab.
“True readiness, however, is impossible unless the government takes the initiative to end the Houthi coup once and for all.”
Ready to shoot
Speaking to The New Arab, fighters and military personnel on the frontlines seem to share the view that an inevitable confrontation is simmering.
A brigadier general leading government-aligned troops on the West Coast front, which encompasses parts of the Taiz and Hodeidah governorates, said that troops in the field are holding their positions while awaiting directives from their leadership on a possible offensive against the Houthis.
“The Houthis have been trying to advance on various fronts, but we have repelled all of their attempts, killing and capturing dozens of them,” he told The New Arab, speaking on condition of anonymity.
“We do not currently have orders to advance into Houthi-controlled territory, but that does not mean we won't: we will do so at the right time.”
He emphasised that government-aligned forces will dictate the timing of the "liberation," claiming that the Houthis have failed to make gains on any front. At present, they are instructed only to return fire, and in many instances, they refrain from responding altogether.
“The battle against the Houthis must be well-prepared, not an impulsive decision. The leadership is currently discussing options, and I am confident they will make the right choice,” the brigadier general said.
Last week, Sheikh Hamoud Al-Mikhlafi, head of the Popular Resistance in Taiz, posted statements on Facebook accounts linked to the movement stating that their forces were ready to advance into Houthi-held areas but were awaiting orders from the PLC.
The Popular Resistance is a collection of pro-government militias formed in 2015 in response to the Houthi takeover of Sanaa.
“Ultimately, a decisive war is inevitable, and I believe it has already begun,” Professor al Mantaser told The New Arab.
“Even if the broader Iran file is not fully resolved, this battle will continue to the end, and any postponement will not last for long."
Carolina Pedrazzi is an investigative conflict reporter specialising in the MENA region with extensive fieldwork experience. She holds a Master's degree from Columbia Journalism School and is a graduate of Sciences Po Paris and the American University of Beirut

Israeli police, govt openly permit Jewish settlers to pray at al-Aqsa in unprecedented escalation

Jewish extremists have regularly carried out raids on the Muslim holy site; however, they are officially prevented from bringing in prayer books and openly performing rituals.

Under the Status Quo agreement governing the holy sites in Jerusalem, worship at the Al-Aqsa Mosque is exclusively for Muslims, with Jews permitted to pray at the Buraq Wall (Western Wall).

Saudi Arabia tightens regulations on money flow to UAE, in latest sign of deepening rift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
10:54:49 UTC
19:54:49 KST

Saudi Arabia has placed financial transfers to the United Arab Emirates under extra layers of regulatory oversight reserved for countries considered high-risk for illicit money flows, according to three people with direct knowledge of the matter, the latest sign of a widening rift between the wealthy Gulf monarchies.
The measures, which were not announced publicly, could help explain why a number of companies say they have had difficulties transferring funds from accounts in Saudi Arabia to the UAE in recent months, an issue first reported by Bloomberg and the Financial Times in July. The enhanced oversight measures have not previously been reported.
Six businesspeople told Reuters their companies have had transfers in various currencies delayed or returned by Saudi banks with no official explanation.
Saudi Arabia's central bank requires financial institutions to apply more checks when dealing with customers or jurisdictions that pose greater risks for money laundering, terrorism financing, and other crimes. Earlier this year, it notified key banks in the country to apply such measures when handling settlements with the UAE, said the three people with direct knowledge of the matter, who, like others, spoke on condition of anonymity.
A fourth person, a Western executive with operations in Saudi Arabia, said they received the same explanation when they asked their bank about transaction delays.
Responding to questions from Reuters, the Saudi central bank said: "There are no direct restrictions on specific countries."
It said Saudi Arabia has a robust regulatory framework to combat money laundering and terrorism financing in line with standards set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), a global watchdog based in Paris.
"All banks in the Kingdom apply necessary controls and preventive measures to mitigate risks based on their own internal assessments and institutional risk appetite, while also assessing various risk factors, including country and geographic risk," it said.
A UAE official said its economy ministry has not received any reports from private-sector companies regarding difficulties or unusual delays in completing bank transfers between the two nations.
"The UAE and Saudi Arabia maintain deep and longstanding economic and commercial ties, supported by significant trade and investment flows," the official said. "We remain in regular engagement with the private sector and relevant stakeholders, and would review any specific concerns brought to our attention through the appropriate channels."
The additional scrutiny puts the UAE – a hub for real estate investment and the trade of precious metals and stones – among more than a half dozen countries in the region deemed high risk in Saudi Arabia for financial crimes, two of the sources said. They include Lebanon, South Sudan, and Iraq, which are on the FATF's "grey list" of jurisdictions that need additional monitoring.
The FATF delisted the UAE in 2024 after it made improvements to its anti-money laundering regime, a decision some anti-corruption groups argue was premature. The United States has imposed sanctions on a number of UAE-based individuals and entities accused of raising or laundering funds for groups such as Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Somalia's al Shabaab militants.
A Saudi insider said the enhanced oversight was intended as a "subtle message" to Emirati leaders about the importance of maintaining good relations following a period of escalating tensions between the two Gulf heavyweights – an interpretation shared by four regional financial-sector sources who were not briefed on the reasons for the measures.
Authorities in Saudi Arabia and the UAE did not answer questions about what may have prompted the move.
The two are major trading partners, but their interests have diverged over the years on everything from oil quotas and geopolitical influence to the race for foreign talent and capital.
UAE, Saudi Arabia clash over Yemen war
Simmering disagreements came into the open late last year over their support for opposing sides in the war in Yemen. Saudi Arabia accused the UAE of threatening its security by backing secessionist forces who made a push toward its borders.
There were more disagreements over how to respond to Iran's war with the United States and Israel, even as Riyadh and Abu Dhabi sought to present a united front against Tehran's attacks on Gulf nations.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE are so deeply enmeshed in trade, investment and logistics that analysts consider a full-blown economic rupture unlikely, saying it would serve neither country's interests. The kingdom is the UAE's largest trading partner in the Arab world, while the UAE was Riyadh's fifth-largest export destination overall and its fourth-largest source of imports in 2024, according to data from the online platform the Observatory of Economic Complexity.
For all their differences, the Iran war has "solidified the rationale for cooperation" to secure vital interests, including reopening the Strait of Hormuz, said Justin Alexander, director of Khalij Economics, a Gulf-focused consultancy.
Top media officials from both nations posted synchronized statements on social media last month underlining the brotherly ties between the two.
Still, economic competition has been brewing for years as both attempt to reduce their reliance on oil-and-gas revenues and establish themselves as world-class financial and business centers.
Saudi Arabia pushing companies to move regional bases to Riyadh
While Dubai remains the Gulf's main business hub, Saudi Arabia has pushed multinational companies to relocate their regional headquarters to Riyadh, making it a condition to secure big government contracts.
The businesspeople who spoke to Reuters said their difficulties with cross-border transfers began in the weeks after the UAE announced on April 28 that it was leaving OPEC, the group of oil-producing states effectively led by Saudi Arabia.
The head of a Dubai-based consultancy said some Saudi clients were struggling to make payments to the firm and had advised him to set up operations elsewhere.
Two other UAE-based companies received similar requests from clients, who said Saudi authorities asked them not to do business with firms in the UAE, according to an investor with stakes in both firms. The companies have been waiting weeks for payments from Saudi Arabia, in some cases for amounts below 1 million dirham ($272,257), which would previously have been processed in a few days, the investor said.
Authorities in Saudi Arabia and the UAE did not respond to questions about these accounts.
Three bankers said the enhanced oversight means transfers to the UAE pass through more hands and receive closer scrutiny from compliance departments. Some transfers take weeks to go through; others never make it, they said.
Three businesspeople said their firms now route payments via third countries to get around the issue.

Ohio firefighters responding to explosions and a fire at Toledo industrial recycling business

Explosions and fire tear through Ohio industrial building, killing 2 workers
TOLEDO, Ohio (AP) — Explosions rocked an Ohio industrial recycling business early Tuesday, killing two workers and sparking a large fire, officials said.
Flames and dark smoke poured from Brent Industries in Toledo as fire engines surrounded the building, TV news video showed.
Crews later discovered the bodies of two employees, a man and a woman, inside the smoldering building, said Toledo Fire Chief Allison Armstrong. Two or three other employees had minor injuries, she said.
Two explosions occurred shortly before 5 a.m., during a shift change, Armstrong said. Crews had to deal with hazardous materials, runoff and the threat of more explosions while first searching for victims and accounting for the other employees, she said.
Environmental officials said monitors showed that there was no hazardous threat in the air.
Demetrius Langston said he felt the explosion half a mile (0.8 kilometers) away. He ran outside with his phone and captured video of a huge plume of smoke rising into the dark sky.
“The shock waves came down the block,” he said. “Then we all heard it again. Boom! You could feel it.”
Armstrong said the fire was still burning Tuesday afternoon. She also said there were no preliminary indications of what caused the explosions.
Aerial images showed that nearly all of the building’s roof was gone and that the blast blew out its walls.
The federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration said it was investigating. The agency has six months to conduct its investigation and it won’t release any more information until that’s completed, officials said.
Authorities encouraged people near the site who could see or smell smoke to keep windows and doors closed and avoid the area.
Phone and email messages were left for Brent Industries.
The company, based in Brent, Alabama, offers textile reconditioning and industrial recycling services aimed at reducing waste and saving money, according to its website. It was founded in Alabama in 1977 and has operations in Brent and Toledo.
The company’s Alabama location also had an explosion and fire in 2015 that killed one person.
After that deadly explosion, OSHA determined that flammable vapor from mineral spirits, a petroleum solvent used for cleaning and other purposes, ignited in an industrial washing machine. The company was cited for a half-dozen violations and fined $27,000, according to OSHA records.
Fire officials say tanks containing mineral spirits were at the Toledo plant. The company says on its website that it uses mineral spirits in the cleaning process for work gloves, wiping clothes and other textiles that contain hazardous substances.
In 2004, OSHA cited Brent Industries for two serious violations at its Toledo plant, including failing to protect workers from death or serious harm when they were exposed to a 207-degree Fahrenheit (97 Celsius) steam release from a washing machine, OSHA records show.

Drug prices have declined sharply, and Trump is taking credit. The reason behind the drop is complex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
10:53:01 UTC
19:53:01 KST

Drug prices have declined sharply, and Trump is taking credit. The reason behind the drop is complex
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump has been taking credit for new federal data that shows U.S. prescription drug prices fell 0.8% in July and are down 3.1% from a year ago, the steepest year-over-year drop since 1963.
The plunging prices, the White House said, resulted from the Republican president’s “most favored nation” drug deals with pharmaceutical firms and the TrumpRx website, which it said are “delivering real relief to American families and putting patients first.”
The real picture is more complicated, said drug pricing experts, who noted that other factors, including a law from Democratic President Joe Biden’s time in office that allowed Medicare to negotiate with pharmaceutical companies, are potentially more significant contributors to the latest consumer price index figures.
Also at play, they said, are generic and biosimilar products that have come onto the market, offering competition that drives down the price of expensive brand-name and biologic drugs. In addition, the prescription drug price index measured by the Labor Department and released last week doesn’t directly reflect how much consumers pay — it measures how much pharmacies get paid for the drugs, both by insurers and consumers.
“It’s difficult to know in one number what’s going on beneath the hood,” said Juliette Cubanski, a vice president and director of the Program on Medicare Policy at the healthcare research nonprofit KFF. “I don’t think we can attribute this price reduction to any one specific policy change or initiative.”
Here’s what to know about the decline in prescription drug prices:
Competition and policy both contribute to changing prices
Drug pricing experts said both market competition and various policy changes have influenced prescription drug prices in recent years.
On the market side, “when big blockbuster products face generic competition, their prices fall,” said Dr. Benjamin Rome, a health policy researcher at Harvard Medical School.
For example, he said, various biosimilar drugs have arrived on the market to treat the same autoimmune conditions as the brand-name drug Humira, offering similar treatment at a lower cost.
Similarly, competition has led to price reductions for Stelara, a popular biologic medicine that treats chronic inflammatory conditions, said Stacie Dusetzina, a professor of health policy at Vanderbilt University School of Medicine.
Biden-era federal policies also likely played a role — most notably the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, which for the first time allowed Medicare to haggle with drugmakers over the cost of the top-selling prescription drugs in the program.
New prices for the first 10 of those negotiated drugs launched in January, a change Cubanski, Rome and Dusetzina all said likely made an impact on aggregate prices. The Trump administration has carried forward those negotiations, as mandated by law, and projects additional savings on prescription drugs in the years ahead.
A new Trump administration policy lowering the price of GLP-1 weight loss drugs for certain eligible Medicare enrollees could also be playing a role in driving down prices, the experts said. But that went into effect in July, so only its first month is reflected in the data.
It’s hard to measure the impact of MFN deals and TrumpRx
Trump has sought to attribute the drop in prescription drug prices to his “most favored nation” deals to bring U.S. pharmaceutical prices to the same level as other developed countries.
Drug pricing experts said the actual impact of those deals so far is unclear, since the contracts with drug companies have not been made public and the models designed to put MFN policies into practice in federal health programs have not gone into effect yet.
“These policies are under development and have not affected payers in the index,” Dusetzina told The Associated Press in an email. “Ultimately, I believe that the change is likely to be more directly related to the IRA’s policies and the Medicare drug price negotiation program than it is to current policies.”
Experts lauded TrumpRx, the White House’s website funneling Americans to the best deals on a variety of prescription drugs, for bringing a helpful resource and more price transparency to the public.
But they said it’s unclear how many Americans are making use of the service. In addition, many of the brand-name drugs it has featured are cheaper with insurance or have lower-cost generic versions sold elsewhere.
The White House said the website has generated $700 million in savings for patients but didn’t explain how it reached that figure. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts last week questioned that claim in a letter to the Trump administration, saying Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has admitted that TrumpRx doesn’t store patient, health or prescription information.
“Without this information, the accuracy of any claim of savings made by the Trump administration is unreliable,” she wrote.
Many consumers still face high drug costs – and rising health costs overall
Even as the consumer price index shows a year-over-year drop in drug prices, experts warned consumers aren’t necessarily seeing that in their budgets.
That’s because the Labor Department’s figures measure not what consumers pay directly but what pharmacies are paid by insurers and consumers. Insurers often eat much of the cost, and what patients pay can depend on a variety of factors, including whether they are insured and what plans they have. Plus, some Americans still rely on expensive drugs that don’t have cheaper alternatives yet.
Higher health spending and federal policy changes are also resulting in higher insurance premiums and out-of-pocket costs for many Americans. That could mean even as drug prices decline, they’re paying more for healthcare than they once were.
“A price measure like the CPI is not going to adequately capture consumers’ experience with healthcare and prescription drugs and other hospital services, the same way it would for groceries and gas and other tangible services that people go and pay for at the store,” Rome said.

CDC’s new director is pressed to do something about its zombie programs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
10:53:01 UTC
19:53:01 KST

The CDC has zombie programs. Congress funds them, but few people are left to do the work
NEW YORK (AP) — The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention still has an Alzheimer’s disease program. Congress appropriated $41 million to it this year. There’s just no one staffing it.
Then there’s the agency’s Office on Smoking and Health. Congress allocated $246 million for that. Its staffers were cut, too.
Same for the epilepsy program. Its sickle cell disease data collection operation. Its rape prevention unit.
Think of them as the CDC’s zombie programs — they appear to be alive, at least according to legislation and congressional appropriations. But functionally they are dead or nearly dead, because the CDC experts who did the work were laid off by President Donald Trump’s administration or remain on leave — paid but not allowed to do their jobs.
The Atlanta-based CDC is charged with protecting Americans from preventable health threats. When Dr. Erica Schwartz became the agency’s latest director last week, she inherited these zombie programs and congressional pressure to bring some of them back to life.
In Schwartz’s confirmation hearing, U.S. Sen. Tim Kaine pressed her to restart the smoking office’s dormant activities.
“This is an office that is in statute, and it’s an office that receives congressional appropriations,” said Kaine, a Virginia Democrat. “Will you follow the law if we appropriate money for this mission and the CDC?”
“I will always follow the law,” Schwartz replied.
Trump officials turned some CDC programs into the living dead
The decision to freeze the programs came from Schwartz’s political bosses.
In April 2025, Trump’s Republican administration sent layoff notices to thousands of employees at the CDC and other federal health agencies. It was part of a sweeping effort to remake the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and consolidate some of its programs under a new subagency called the Administration for a Healthy America. That reorganization hasn’t happened, amid congressional pushback.
But the layoffs did. Led by then-adviser Elon Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency, the cuts affected researchers, scientists, doctors, support staffers and senior leaders, leaving the government without many of the key experts who long guided U.S. decisions on medical research, drug approvals and other issues.
The cuts were challenged in lawsuits and through pleas to legislators.
Some were reversed. Drastic cuts to the CDC’s National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, for example, were rescinded. Other reinstatements included staffers at labs that test for sexually transmitted diseases and support lead poisoning control.
But many of the cuts endured. As a result of litigation, staffers who initially were laid off have been placed on administrative leave while the fight moves through the legal system, paid to not do their jobs.
Not all public health efforts associated with every impacted program stopped. Most of the CDC’s budget is passed on to state and local programs, and much of grant processing has continued.
Staffers at the CDC and other federal health agencies “deserve a lot of credit for getting money out the door,” said Eric Gascho, executive director of the Coalition for Health Funding.
But gone are seasoned experts doing research into the health threats, assessing which grant-funded programs work and which don’t and setting a national framework for best ways to save and prolong lives.
“Without the experts, the coordination is not there across the country” in tackling public health problems, said Erika Sward, chief advocacy officer for UsAgainstAlzheimer’s. “You’re often flying blind, and without a parachute, when you don’t have the CDC staff in place.”
A union is keeping track of the zombie programs
In January, Congress passed an appropriations bill, which became law, that specified funding for more than 200 projects and activities. The law requires that HHS maintain staff to carry out statutorily required program work, although it does not say how many staffers must be in each program to do it.
Since then, current and former CDC employees have compiled a list of dozens of funded-but-decimated CDC programs. They include:
— The Office on Smoking and Health, which tracked trends, supported quit lines and operated the “Tips from Former Smokers” ad campaign that researchers associate with billions of dollars in saved healthcare costs.
— A $41 million Alzheimer’s initiative for better surveillance, risk prevention and communications campaigns. Affected work includes development of a webpage that was to explain what’s known about a potential link between menopause and Alzheimer’s disease, whether early menopause is related to higher risk and whether hormone therapy can lessen that risk.
— An $18 million program to support overdose prevention in tribal communities.
— An $11 million program focused on tracking epilepsy and community programs that help people manage the condition.
— A sickle cell disease data collection program, for which Congress appropriated $6 million.
— The Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System, the most comprehensive collection of data on the health behaviors and outcomes before, during and after childbirth. Researchers have been using its data to investigate the nation’s maternal mortality problem.
— A $2 million program focused on preventing drownings.
Notably, the cuts affected a number of programs focused on the causes and prevention of chronic diseases. U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said tackling chronic disease is his central priority, and he has faulted the CDC for not doing enough.
Democrats say what’s happening at the CDC is illegal
After President Richard Nixon, a Republican, refused to spend appropriated funds, Congress passed the Impoundment Control Act in 1974. The CDC’s zombie programs represent a violation of that law, Democratic lawmakers say.
But there is no appropriations police or law enforcement agency that Congress can use to enforce the law. Republicans control the House and the Senate, so there’s been limited appetite for Congress to challenge the Trump administration.
“President Trump is showing time and again that he will put politics ahead of Americans’ health — and sadly, my Republican colleagues continue to look the other way,” said U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin, a Wisconsin Democrat, in a statement.
In a spending bill passed this year, Baldwin and other senators included new requirements that federal health agencies maintain staffing levels necessary to fulfill statutory responsibilities, but the bill did not specify staffing levels for each program.
Sen. Jon Ossoff is a Democrat who represents Georgia, where the CDC is based. He suggested legislators are watching whether Schwartz will administer the programs that Congress funded.
“We will learn swiftly whether she intends to follow the law,” he said in a statement.
Plans to hire people have not revived the programs
Kennedy visited the CDC earlier this month. An Associated Press reporter heard a recording of an employee forum at which Kennedy praised CDC employees and told them: “My sole purpose is to allow you to do your jobs.” He didn’t address the funded programs that have no staff.
In April, Kennedy said in a congressional hearing that more workers were needed at federal health agencies, and he planned to hire 12,000 people — mainly to address chronic health conditions.
It’s unclear how many have been hired at the CDC since then. U.S. health officials did not respond to a question about that.
Apparently there’s been very little, suggested an official with the American Federation of Government Employees, a union representing CDC employees.
“Not only have we not had any … really significant hiring of CDC employees, but we’ve also had ignoring and stalling when it comes to those employees that had been (laid off), who were supposed to have priority for some of those jobs,” said AFGE Local 2883 President Yolanda Jacobs.
Schwartz started at the CDC last week. The AP requested her comment on her plans regarding the programs.
The response came from an HHS spokesperson, who emailed: “Dr. Schwartz is determined to support and empower employees to ensure they have what they need to succeed.”

"The power output of this advanced powerplant – the first of its kind in Russia – will be 1,450 horsepower," the statement said. Since existing key components are being used as the basis for this project, this accelerates the development process, Rostec added.
According to the state corporation, the use of a modern FADEC-type electronic control system will ensure stable engine operation at altitudes ranging from 300 to 4,500 meters, at 100% relative humidity and temperatures ranging from -50 to +55 degrees Celsius.
Rostec added that the UEC has already developed the new-generation PD-8 and TV7-117ST-01 engines for regional airliners, the PD-14 for medium-range aircraft, and is currently developing a family of solutions based on the PD-35 for long-range aircraft. "Small aircraft have not been forgotten either: the VK-1600S is designed for small passenger aircraft, such as the TVS-2DTS. It can also be used for the An-2 and An-3 – there are still many of these aircraft in Russia, so there is a need for new engines," the company noted.
In July, the Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya) issued a certificate for the An-2 aircraft, according to the agency’s head, Dmitry Yadrov. The certificate will allow for the modernization and modification of the aircraft, Deputy Industry and Trade Minister Gennady Abramenkov said. According to Rosaviatsiya, there are currently 49 An-2s in commercial service in Russia and 358 used for aerial work.
