England’s children’s commissioner says Prevent failing to help young people ‘fixated with violence’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:20:07 UTC
18:20:07 KST

The children’s commissioner for England has warned of a group of children “intoxicated by extremism” who need help the UK government’s anti-terror programme cannot provide.
Referrals to Prevent – the programme designed to safeguard vulnerable people from being radicalised or drawn into extremism – involving children have risen in the past decade, from 2,918 in 2016-17 to 4,715 in 2024-25.
Axel Rudakubana, who when aged 17 killed three girls at a dance class and tried to murder eight other girls and two adults in the Southport attack in July 2024, had been referred to Prevent three times, but his case was closed over a lack of clear ideology.
The chair of the inquiry into that attack has previously said officers were “hampered” by a lack of clarity on whether they should take someone on who demonstrated signs of being fixated on violence but without adherence to a particular ideology.
In a new report, published on Tuesday, the children’s commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, said the current process “risks missing opportunities” and called for a “stronger safeguarding response particularly for children who are fixated with violence but have no identified extremist ideology”.
“It is clear that we have a cohort of children becoming intoxicated by extremism, radicalisation or a desire to harm others, who need interventions that Prevent is not able to provide,” she said in the report.
Her office’s analysis suggested seven in 10 (71%) of referrals to Prevent involved children who did not have a clear ideology, with many linked to exposure to harmful content online such as videos of violence, discussion of weapons and sharing of extreme pornography.
Of the total Prevent referrals for children between April 2024 and March 2025, 79% were closed without progressing through the programme.
In this time period, almost 60% of Prevent referrals came from education providers, while police accounted for 20% and local authorities 11%.
But the commissioner’s office found that at least 65% of referrals from education providers were referred back to them on closing, the vast majority of which (93%) had not progressed any further through the Prevent programme.
Her report said: “This highlights that there is a group of children which professionals are greatly concerned about, and seeking support for, but are finding closed doors and dead ends.”
Among her report’s recommendations, de Souza has called for the Home Office and Department for Education to issue joint statutory guidance on children who pose a risk to others.
She said this should require all children deemed to be violence-fixated, or where there are concerns around being drawn into terrorism or other criminality, to be referred to local authority safeguarding teams alongside Prevent.
The assessment teams should “act as a ‘triage’ for all these children, including drawing on expertise from counter-terror police at the initial assessment stage when concerns about terrorism are identified, and then children should be allocated to the appropriate intervention from there”.
A government spokesperson said: “We are committed to ensuring all children are safe from radicalisation and Prevent plays a crucial role in this, moving more than 6,000 people away from violent ideologies since 2015.
“Every Prevent referral is assessed thoroughly by experts. If it’s determined a person is not at risk of being drawn into terrorism, it is right they are supported by other, more appropriate services.
“We thank the children’s commissioner for her report. We are reviewing it alongside our work in response to the Southport inquiry, including developing further options to manage those fascinated with extreme violence.”

EU packaging rule change prompts confusion, online shops halt foreign orders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:20:00 UTC
18:20:00 KST

EU packaging rule change prompts confusion, online shops halt foreign orders
Since last Wednesday, a new packaging and packaging‑waste regulation has been in force in the European Union. One of the changes requires businesses to register in the producer register of every member state where they sell goods.
The new regulation is raising many questions among small entrepreneurs, and several producers have shut down foreign ordering options in their online stores until they receive clear answers.
Kaidi Holm, who works daily with legal counseling and training for NGOs, has been operating for three years as a small entrepreneur — owner, manager and sole employee of Seebistuudio. In addition to Estonia, her largest target market has been Finland, and her soaps could previously be ordered anywhere through her online store.
"Now, when we're supposed to start applying this regulation country by country, we've decided to close deliveries to other countries in the online store. We're waiting until we have fully researched what the exact obligation is and what it entails," Holm said.
According to her, reducing packaging waste is already an important priority for small businesses in this field. However, paperwork should be tied to the size of the company, and micro‑enterprises should be exempt from this burden.
"The main obstacle for a small business is that when there are few people who already have many different roles, one additional obligation means taking time away from other tasks. The administrative burden is exactly the same for someone who occasionally makes a bit of soap as it is for a large company," Holm said.
The packaging regulation affects all businesses that sell packaged goods on the EU market. This includes Luunja cucumbers, the chemical industry, and small designers' products. A‑Gallery, which represents Estonia's professional jewelry artists, also shut down its online store until there is clarity about what is allowed and certainty that foreign sales will not result in hefty fines.
"We would actually expect a more official approach, not just 'keep running your business.' How do we get this law in order so that we don't have to fear that we're operating as if illegally," said jewelry artist and A‑Gallery board chair Valdek Laur.
Deputy Secretary General at the Ministry of Climate, Ivo Jaanisoo, does not see a reason to stop sales activity.
"The packaging regulation actually enters into force with a transition period. Right now, Europe is discussing the relevant implementing act — what reporting and data submission should look like. When this implementing act enters into force, presumably later this year, member states will still have a year and a half to bring their registers into compliance," Jaanisoo said.

One of the attacks was directed at a house in the centre of the city. The munition dropped by the drone flew through a window into the room where the boy was sleeping.
The boy's mother immediately took him to the nearest hospital. Their lives are not in danger, and police officers and volunteers are now arranging their evacuation.
"Law enforcement officers also removed the munition from the child's bed and documented the latest war crime committed by the army of the aggressor state.
Once again, we urge families with children to evacuate from areas that are being systematically attacked by the enemy. There are no limits to the enemy's cruelty," the police stressed.
Background:
- On the night of 11-12 February, a Russian attack on Dnipro caused a fire to break out in a house and the ceiling collapsed onto a baby's cot. The baby had been taken out just in time.
- Serhii, a neighbour of the family, said: "The baby started crying or something, so the mother went over and picked the child up. She took three steps away, and then the ceiling came down right onto the cot."

'Niu Lai': How is a 'disaster-level' Chinese animated film rivalling 'The Odyssey' at the box-office?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:16:12 UTC
18:16:12 KST

A low-budget and shoddy-looking animated film has emerged as this summer’s most unexpected box-office hit in China. Here’s how ‘Niu Lai’ has transformed online mockery into big bucks and a viral phenomenon.
There are films that fall under the "so bad, it's good" category... And then there's "ugly", "eerie", "godawful" and "disaster-level".
Those are some of the terms used to describe Niu Lai ('Here Comes The Cow'), a new Chinese animated film directed by Xin Yumeng and produced by Dalian Jingyuan Culture Film and Television Media, formerly an interior design and decoration company.
The film has been ridiculed for its shoddy animation and low-quality effects, and has even faced calls for theatres to stop screening it.
However, in a surprising turn of events, the film has gained sudden notoriety.
Niu Lai started its theatrical rollout with poor box office numbers and scathing reviews, with the stiff animation, poor voice acting and an abstract plot about a newborn calf growing up and coming to terms with love and sacrifice being the main points of criticism. But word of mouth and mockery soon transformed it into a viral sensation on Chinese social media.
From earning only about 10,000 yuan (approx. €1,281) at the box office in the first 10 days after its 5 August release – with some days tallying as little as 200 yuan (€25) at the box office, according to movie-tracking platform Maoyan – Niu Lai ’s box office surged to 8.2 million yuan (more than €1 million) as of Monday. Its total box office has reached 17.1 million yuan (€2.1 million).
As a result, the film is even rivalling Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey and is now among the top ten highest-grossing animated films in China in 2026.
So, what gives?
Despite the flood of criticism and memes, some viewers have embraced the rudimentary animation and have started recommending the film as either a prank or a genuine antidote to AI slop taking over social media algorithms. Indeed, the handmade easthetic has apparently resonated with audiences, who champion Niu Lai as a welcome remedy for overly polished studio animation.
Quite where the irony stops and starts is still up for debate...
Regardless, countless fans have begun sharing clips of Niu Lai, praising its low-budget verve and complimenting Xin Yumeng and Sun Lifang, reportedly a mother-and-son team who made Niu Lai over the course of five years and served as the film’s writers, voice actors, and principal crew.
Others simply said they wanted to see it to find out "just how bad it could be" and joked that Nolan must be flabbergasted to witness that Niu Lai is becoming the unlikely rival to The Odyssey – which opened in China on 14 August.
It has proved so popular that cinemas have added screenings of the film in response to soaring demand, proving that all it takes is some social media buzz to elevate your film to certified hit status.
Predictably, some aren't so thrilled at the film's unexpected box office achievement, arguing that Niu Lai 's popularity comes at the expense of more accomplished productions.
For instance, state-owned Beijing News warned that cinemas risk "losing the trust" of viewers if they "continue to lower their standard" with additional screenings of Niu Lai.
The outlet urged cinemas to "act as gatekeepers for the audience, and clearly reject films that are obviously not up to standard instead of letting films like Niu Lai run rampant".
Spoilsports. Whether audiences are laughing at or with the film, Niu Lai has managed to turn mockery into a theatrical success story - as well as one of the highest returns on investment for a Chinese film. Your move, Odysseus.

Pakistan top court orders Imran Khan’s hospital transfer amid access battle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:15:03 UTC
18:15:03 KST

Pakistan top court orders Imran Khan’s hospital transfer amid access battle
Supreme Court grants jailed ex-PM transfer to hospital for nearly a month after concerns are raised over his blood pressure.
Islamabad, Pakistan – Pakistan’s Supreme Court has ordered the transfer of Imran Khan, former prime minister and founder of the opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party, from Rawalpindi’s Adiala prison to Islamabad’s Shifa International Hospital within two days, granting a demand his party had been making for months.
Uzair Bhandari, one of Khan’s lawyers, told Al Jazeera the three-member bench on Tuesday also ordered a medical board be formed to oversee Khan’s treatment, including the former prime minister’s sister Dr Uzma Khan and his personal physician Dr Faisal Sultan.
“The court also directed that Khan’s family be allowed to meet him at the hospital and that he be permitted to speak with his sons, who live abroad,” Bhandari said.
The next hearing has been scheduled for September 16, and Khan should remain hospitalised until at least then as per the order, according to the lawyer. This would be the longest period Khan would be physically outside jail premises since he was imprisoned in August 2023 and convicted in several corruption-related cases that he and his party insist are politically motivated.
The order followed a report that Adiala jail’s superintendent submitted to the court on Monday, detailing a cardiac board’s August 10 review of Khan, 73, which recorded fluctuating blood pressure and anxiety linked to what it said was restricted contact with his family.
During Tuesday’s hearing, the court pressed Pakistan’s advocate general over gaps in the report, saying Khan’s “pulse and heart condition were not normal” and his vital organs “had started being affected”.
Courts had twice declined similar transfer requests since February, including an Islamabad High Court ruling that ordered a medical board’s assessment instead.
Zulfi Bukhari, a senior PTI leader, told Al Jazeera the ruling reinforced the party’s longstanding position that Khan needed independent, specialised treatment outside Adiala jail.
“Medical care provided within the prison system is no substitute for a thorough evaluation by independent specialists of his choosing,” Bukhari said, adding that the PTI had consistently called for Khan’s transfer to Shifa International Hospital and access to his own doctors.
Government officials have insisted any transfer requires judicial authorisation rather than executive discretion.
Rana Sanaullah, adviser to Prime Minister Shebaz Sharif, told the Senate on Monday that Khan was receiving “the best available medical treatment” and his condition did not support the PTI’s concerns.
The order was issued amid a wider standoff over access to Khan, which the PTI has increasingly framed as the condition for reviving talks with the government.
The government said it has renewed its efforts to engage in dialogue with little success while the PTI leadership has announced a countrywide protest on September 27.
PTI’s next move
The PTI has urged its supporters to not gather outside Shifa International Hospital, calling in a statement for a “peaceful environment” around the facility during Khan’s treatment.
Aleema Khan, one of Khan’s sisters, spoke to reporters outside the court on Tuesday, where she said the family had assured the bench it would not discuss the case’s substance publicly, a condition attached to the hearing.
“There came a time when we had become completely hopeless,” she said, “But in that very state, God opened a path of justice for us.”
After Tuesday’s court order, PTI spokesman Sheikh Waqas Akram told Al Jazeera that preparations for the September 27 march “will go on regardless of whatever else happens”.
“He [Khan] has instructed us to strive for justice and rule of law. That is our bigger goal, and we will continue our preparations for that,” Akram said.
He said the party will reconsider its future actions only if the government complies with court orders and opens talks that acknowledge what the PTI calls a “theft of mandate” in the 2024 elections.
“If they don’t do that, we have no choice but to go on with our march,” he said.
In a post on X, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province Chief Minister and senior PTI leader Sohail Afridi called the court’s order “a justice-based, appreciable decision” and said the PTI “will not do any politics” over Khan’s health.
Signs of a thaw?
Some analysts saw signs of reconciliation between the government and Pakistan’s main opposition party.
“In the past, there have been plenty of rumours about a deal that went nowhere, but this time, there are a few signs of a possible thaw with PTI,” said Benazir Shah, a Lahore-based political analyst.
“With security challenges in Balochistan piling up and protests in Azad Jammu and Kashmir, delaying a confrontation with PTI in the capital could certainly help buy the government some breathing room,” she told Al Jazeera.
The southwestern province of Balochistan, Pakistan’s largest by area and most sparsely populated, saw hundreds of attacks this year.
Pakistan-administered Kashmir has also seen months of unrest since authorities banned a civil society coalition demanding electoral and economic reforms. Violence surrounding last month’s regional elections killed dozens of people.
But Shah cautioned against reading too much into the signs of a thaw, adding that any reconciliation would hinge on Khan himself.
“He remains the central figure in PTI, and any [government] deal with the party would ultimately require his approval,” she said.
“If he is moved to hospital and allowed greater access to other party leaders, only then would it be clear whether he is prepared to engage with the existing political and military set-up.”

U.S. Destroyer USS Benfold Lost Power for Four Days in the South China Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:14:44 UTC
18:14:44 KST

The U.S. destroyer USS Benfold was without power for four days while conducting routine operations in the Indo-Pacific region, the U.S. Navy’s 7th Fleet told CNN.
On July 24, due to an engineering malfunction in the generators, the ship lost its ability to maneuver independently and was left without toilets, air conditioning, a functioning galley, and drinking water production.
The Navy did not specify the exact location of the accident. However, according to USNI News, the destroyer was in the South China Sea. In late July, daytime temperatures in that area ranged from about 32 to 37 °C.
During the incident, the guided-missile cruiser USS Robert Smalls assisted USS Benfold by providing the crew with ready-to-eat meals. Other ships in the USS George Washington carrier strike group also assisted the destroyer during those days.
Eventually, the Benfold was towed to a bay in the Philippines for repairs. The U.S. Navy stated that the repairs were completed by August 8, after which the ship returned to active duty.
The cause of the generator failure is currently under investigation. This is the second such incident involving a U.S. Navy destroyer in the Indo-Pacific region this year: in April, the USS Higgins also lost power and the ability to maneuver for several hours due to an electrical system malfunction.
Due to the heavy strain on the U.S. Navy caused by the war in the Middle East, reports of operational difficulties affecting various types of vessels are becoming increasingly common.
USS Benfold and USS Higgins are both Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, which form the backbone of the U.S. Navy’s surface fleet. It has more than 70 such destroyers in service.
USS Benfold is typically part of the group accompanying USS George Washington, an aircraft carrier currently en route to the Middle East to replace USS Abraham Lincoln.
The crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln experienced a sharp decline in morale after more than 250 days at sea without a proper port call.
The sailors are working long shifts, have already spent about 40 days in continuous combat operations, and are facing disruptions in supplies, mail, food, and water. Against this backdrop, their relatives report a decline in morale and instances of suicidal thoughts.
Aircraft carriers typically call at port every 30-45 days to restock supplies, undergo maintenance, and give the crew time to rest.
The carrier was originally scheduled for a routine deployment in the Pacific region but was diverted to the Middle East due to hostilities. This disrupted normal logistics routes, and the crew was unable to take regular rest periods in port.
The Navy is working to restore normal supply operations and has already managed to provide the aircraft carrier with the necessary supplies during a brief stopover in Oman.

Finnish companies experiment with shorter working hours
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:14:38 EEST
18:14:38 KST

The Finnish Confederation of Professionals (STTK) is once again opening a debate on shortening working hours.
A report published on Tuesday concludes that working life is continuing to change, with shorter working hours among the developments taking place. It says innovative and flexible workplaces could turn new ways of working into a significant competitive advantage.
Taina Vallander, who leads STTK's social impact team, says the discussion should focus less on whether working hours should be shorter or longer and more on how work itself is changing.
"We are approaching the discussion about shortening working hours from the perspective of how we can improve employees' well-being and commitment, maintain their ability to work, and possibly extend their careers or distribute work differently," Vallander says.
Examples of different hours
The report highlights four Finnish companies that have introduced different forms of shorter working hours.
Oulu-based game developer Fingersoft, best known for its Hill Climb Racing game, offers employees the option of working 80 percent of full-time hours. Around 25–30 percent of its staff currently use the option.
Employees working a four-day week receive 80 percent of their normal salary, while those working six-hour days get 90 percent.
Similalry, most employees at Tampere restaurant Kajo work four days a week on full pay, while vehicle electronics company Sercap in Keminmaa has also introduced a four-day week with full pay.
Helsinki-based consultancy Third Rock gives employees Friday afternoons off without reducing their salaries, as CEO Leo Stranius believes Friday afternoons can be relatively unproductive, as employees may already be thinking about their weekend plans.
Reducing the strain of night work
Vallander believes shorter working hours could be the next major step in developing working life.
One of STTK's most concrete proposals is to reduce the strain caused by night work.
In Norway, some care workers on night shifts work fewer hours while receiving the same pay. Vallander says the arrangement can help reduce the health risks and strain associated with working at night.
She also suggests shorter working hours could be tested when employees are going through particularly demanding periods in their lives.
Shorter hours work best in "good workplaces"
Anna Kuokkanen, the researcher who wrote the STTK report, says more experimentation is needed to understand how shorter working hours affect workplaces.
She says the model works best in workplaces where employees and management can rethink how work is organised and where there is good communication and team spirit.
"The employees get involved in thinking about how working hours could be reduced and participate in planning how it would be implemented," Kuokkanen says.
She adds that a trial does not commit an employer to making the arrangement permanent.
"If you agree on a trial period of six months or a year, you can then decide how to proceed based on the results. It can help workplaces find better ways of organising work," Kuokkanen says.

Iraq arrests senior PMF figure amid disarmament push
Unknown

2026-08-18

Breadcrumb
Iraq arrests senior PMF intelligence official amid disarmament push
Iraqi security forces have detained a senior commander in the Iran-aligned Harakat al-Nujaba group, in a move that could intensify tensions between the government and armed factions resisting efforts to bring weapons under state control.
Abbas Hussein al-Yaqoubi, a senior Nujaba figure who also serves as an intelligence official within Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), was detained on Monday in the southern province of Dhi Qar, according to Iraqi officials and security sources.
Security sources in Baghdad told The New Arab that a special unit linked to Iraq's Counter Terrorism Service raided a residential building about 360 kilometres south of Baghdad and detained Yaqoubi.
Helicopters and armoured vehicles accompanied the force during the operation, according to one security source. The unit subsequently left Dhi Qar for Baghdad without clashes.
The Iraqi News Agency also reported Yaqoubi's detention, identifying him as the intelligence chief for Harakat al-Nujaba and an intelligence director for the PMF's Baghdad Belt Operations Command.
The PMF, however, said Yaqoubi had voluntarily surrendered to the authorities.
No official reason for the arrest was immediately disclosed.
But a former Iraqi lawmaker from the Fatah Alliance told The New Arab that the detention was linked to investigations into drone attacks carried out in recent months. He provided no further details.
Yaqoubi has also been accused of involvement in attacks targeting US forces in Iraq.
Platforms affiliated with Iraqi armed factions described the detention as a "kidnapping" and called for demonstrations in the Fadhiliya area of Nasiriyah, the capital of Dhi Qar province.
Pressure over militia weapons
The arrest comes at a particularly sensitive moment for Iraq's government as a late-September deadline approaches for bringing weapons under state control.
Several armed factions linked to the PMF have categorically rejected surrendering their weapons while US forces remain in Iraq, raising the prospect of a confrontation with the government.
Harakat al-Nujaba, led by Akram al-Kaabi, is among Iraq's most powerful Iran-aligned armed factions. The United States has designated the group a terrorist organisation.
The detention could become an early test of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's willingness and ability to confront factions refusing to comply with the government's disarmament push.
Othman al-Shaibani, a member of the Iraqi parliament's Security and Defence Committee, recently described warnings issued by Zaidi over the weapons issue as "extremely serious".
In a televised interview, Shaibani said the prime minister had warned that if Iraqi institutions failed to disarm armed groups themselves, outside powers, particularly the United States, could take matters into their own hands.
"Zaidi clearly warned that if national institutions are unable to carry out their duties in disarming the factions, the international community, particularly the American side, will undertake the task itself," Shaibani said.
Such intervention would not necessarily be limited to political pressure, he added, warning that it could escalate to strikes and targeted killings against faction positions.
The government, Shaibani noted, was seeking to avoid such a scenario by resolving the issue domestically and bringing armed groups under state authority.
'Last chance' before 30 September
According to Shaibani, Zaidi has warned that failure to address the armed factions could expose Iraq to international isolation and severe economic consequences, potentially including restrictions on financial transfers and the flow of oil revenues.
Such measures could ultimately affect Baghdad's ability to meet its financial obligations and pay public-sector salaries, he said.
Shaibani also claimed the prime minister had warned of the possibility of renewed international oversight of Iraq and a return to measures associated with Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter, which he said would undermine the country's sovereignty.
The government views 30 September as a "last chance" to avoid those consequences, according to Shaibani.
He said Zaidi had expressed a willingness to confront any group refusing to surrender its weapons and viewed bringing arms under state control as non-negotiable, "whatever the cost, even his life".
Yaqoubi's detention could bring that confrontation closer.
With some of Iraq's most powerful armed factions insisting they will not disarm as long as American troops remain in the country, the arrest of a senior Nujaba figure risks becoming more than an isolated security operation, and instead an early indication of how far Baghdad is prepared to go to enforce its deadline.

Rhine drought, heatwaves and deaths: Is it time for Germany to enshrine climate protection in law?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:13:32 UTC
18:13:32 KST

Germany’s coalition government is split over putting climate protection in the constitution.
A debate is heating up in Germany over whether to enshrine climate protection in the constitution.
The proposal by a group of German ministers sparked pushback from within the government on 17 August, despite Western Europe sweltering through record-breaking summer temperatures – with a litany of ill effects.
Germany alone has recorded around 12,500 heat-related deaths in 2026 so far. The country has also temporarily relaxed truck-driving restrictions to ease pressure on supply chains disrupted by record-low water levels on the Rhine.
Climate scientists say global warming is intensifying drought and wildfires, dropping river levels and threatening harvests in Europe's biggest economy.
German ministers say law limits response to climate crisis
Ministers from the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD), junior coalition partners to Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservatives, said Berlin must enshrine the need for "climate adaptation and nature conservation" in the German constitution, known as the Basic Law.
They urged changes to urban planning legislation and building codes, and new labour laws to address working in high temperatures.
With the Rhine running low and forest fires flaring, the SPD's Environmental Minister Carsten Schneider said the climate crisis was now a "tangible reality" but that current law limits what his ministry can do in response.
Key figures in Merz's CDU/CSU bloc were however lukewarm on the idea, warning about the potential costs.
Klaus Mack, deputy chairman of the CDU's parliamentary group, raised concerns about possible fiscal implications and administrative hurdles.
The CDU's climate policy spokesman, Mark Helfrich, told Politico that they "are not convinced" by the SPD idea of new joint funding for national, regional and local climate measures.
Who supports a German climate protection law?
Environmental groups largely voiced support for the SPD proposal and criticised Merz for not laying out a plan of his own about how to address drought, heat and water shortages.
"This summer of extremes shows that Germany is ill-prepared for the heatwaves striking us with increasing frequency due to the escalating climate crisis," Barbara Metz, head of Environmental Action Germany (DUH), told the RND media group.
The opposition Greens in principle also back the idea – but their party chief Felix Banaszak charged that the SPD had previously blocked similar proposals and warned voters: "Don't fall for these con artists."
Climate action "is not rocket science", he added, demanding more renewable energy and grid and storage capacity to make Germany "independent of fossil fuel imports".
Is Germany backsliding on climate commitments?
Merz has faced accusations of backsliding on Germany's robust climate commitments, as he has sought to bolster the economy by cutting red tape and bringing down energy costs.
An expert commission in May forecast that Germany would miss its 2030 greenhouse gas emissions targets, which are anchored in law.
DUH – which successfully sued the previous government over a climate plan that courts determined was inadequate – has also brought a lawsuit over the current government's climate action plan.
The SPD plan would require support from Merz's conservatives, as amending the Basic Law requires a two-thirds majority in parliament.
The far-left Die Linke party dismissed the proposal as "empty promises" while the far-right and climate-sceptic AfD categorically rejected it.
Other European countries are debating similar reforms.
In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's leftist government in June unveiled a programme to strengthen "resilience to heatwaves, floods, droughts and other risks posed by climate change".
It calls for sweeping measures such as a national network of climate shelters and more urban greenery, but it is not clear whether it can get the necessary consensus and money to implement it.

Tornado tears through western Russian city (VIDEOS)
A tornado swept through the western Russian city of Nizhny Novgorod on Monday as a powerful storm brought torrential rain and flooding.
Footage shared online showed a dark funnel descending from storm clouds and hurling debris into the air.
The downpour overwhelmed drainage systems, with local media describing it as a wall of rain that turned some streets into fast-moving streams.
Trees and large branches were brought down by strong winds, with some reportedly landing on parked vehicles and damaging windows and bodywork.
No injuries were reported, according to Nizhny Novgorod Mayor Yury Shalabayev, who said municipal crews had been dispatched to deal with the aftermath.
The severe weather came amid an unusually sharp cold snap, with temperatures in Nizhny Novgorod plunging to around 8C (46F), well below the mid-August norm, when daytime highs typically reach around 22C (72F).
The Nizhny Novgorod tornado was the latest in a series of extreme weather events recorded in Russia this summer. In June, a powerful vortex tore through the Ural town of Kushva, injuring 16 people, while a twister in Perm Region in late May destroyed more than 700 hectares of forest.
A major climatological study found that on average more than 100 tornadoes were recorded annually in Russia between 2009 and 2018, although most occurred away from densely populated areas. Researchers say their frequency had historically been significantly underestimated.

China’s growth expectations ease as economy loses momentum in July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:12:55 UTC
18:12:55 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu, Emirhan Yilmaz, and Emir Yildirim
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
China’s worse-than-expected 4.5% yearly rise in industrial production in July, following a 5.3% rise the previous month, showed that the country’s economy lost momentum, while consumer spending slowed and urban investments contracted.
Coupled with unemployment climbing to 5.2% in July from 5% in June, the situation showed that industrial production is slowing and weakness in domestic demand and the real estate sector continues.
The Chinese National Bureau of Statistics’ failure to release the data at the expected time also fueled concerns over the health of the world’s second-largest economy.
The situation also contributed to expectations that the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) may cut rates.
China’s retail sales climbed 0.6% in July, below estimates, following a 1% rise in June, while fixed-asset investments fell 6.7% at the same time.
China’s real estate investments fell 19.2% year-on-year in July, and residential real estate sales dropped 13.2%.
 
 
Chinese industrial production remains strong despite easing
 
Sadi Kaymaz, an Asian markets analyst, told Anadolu that China’s industrial production remains relatively resilient as the country’s industrial robot production surged 30% and integrated circuit production jumped 21%.
Kaymaz stated that there was a slowdown in nearly every category except high-tech manufacturing sectors and that the slowdown has become a trend by now, as extreme weather events last month affected logistics centers and warehouses in some regions of the country.
He noted that government officials might deem the July data a short-lived setback and wait for the August data to be released.
“China may not see the 4.5% economic growth target and growth could drop to around 4%,” he said.
Kaymaz mentioned that Chinese Premier Li Qiang called for accelerating the country’s new growth drivers.
“Beijing is approaching growth via qualitatitve assesment rather than quantitative figures, and it seems content with high-tech manufacturing developments, so that’s why we don’t expect a significant stimulus package,” he said, noting that even if a package was announced, it would be aimed at meeting the minimum growth target of 4.5%.
“The Politburo met at the end of last month and the deterioration in leading indicators was one of the main agenda items but no stimulus measures were announced,” he added.

Suspected Israeli strikes hit Syria airbase after Turkish visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:12:49 UTC
18:12:49 KST

Breadcrumb
US rebukes Israel over Syria strikes after Turkish military visit
Israeli warplanes struck a military airport in northwestern Syria early on Tuesday, hours after a Turkish military delegation visited the site to begin preparations to rehabilitate its runways, in an attack that appeared to send a message to Ankara over its role in rebuilding Syria's military capabilities.
The strikes on Abu al-Duhur military airport, in the eastern countryside of Syria's Idlib province, drew condemnation from Damascus and a rare public rebuke from Washington, with US special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack describing the attack as an "unnecessary escalation" that did not serve regional stability.
The attack marked the first on the site since the fall of the Assad regime and the first Israeli airstrike in Syria since March.
A source in the Syrian Ministry of Defence told The New Arab that Israeli aircraft carried out the attack. Israel has not claimed responsibility.
The source said two strikes hit the airport's runway at around 2:50 AM local time, causing damage but no injuries or fatalities.
Syrian state-run Al-Ekhbariya, citing a military source, reported that warplanes carried out a total of eight strikes on the airport, damaging its runways. Al Jazeera separately reported four strikes on the runway.
Abu al-Duhur is the second-largest military airport in northern Syria. The sprawling facility covers around eight square kilometres and has 22 runways.
The timing of the attack, coming just hours after Turkish military officials inspected the site, has raised questions over whether Israel was seeking to warn Ankara against helping Syria rebuild its air force.
Informed sources told The New Arab that a Turkish military delegation had visited the airport on Monday as part of initial plans to rehabilitate its runways, stressing that the project remained in its early stages.
Several Turkish vehicles were still on the airport premises at the time, the sources said, while a reconnaissance aircraft was also operating in the area.
Following the Turkish delegation's visit on Monday, an Israeli reconnaissance aircraft flew over the military airport later that evening and into the early hours of Tuesday, according to the sources. The strikes followed around dawn.
The sequence suggests Israel had been closely monitoring activity at the airport ahead of the attack, with the timing pointing to a possible message to Turkey as Ankara moves to assist Syria in rebuilding its military and air capabilities.
US voices 'deep concern' over Israeli strikes
In Washington's first reaction to the attack, US special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack expressed "deep concern" over the confirmed Israeli airstrikes on Abu al-Duhur, calling them an "unnecessary escalation" that did not serve regional stability.
Barrack pointed to the approach taken by the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, saying Damascus "has not adopted a hostile posture nor maintained proxy forces, but has repeatedly demonstrated a preference for de-escalation with Israel".
He also emphasised Washington's efforts to reduce tensions between the two countries.
The United States, Barrack said, "has in the past, and will continue in the future, to host discussions to encourage a diplomatic rhythm rather than military frustration for both countries".
Sustainable de-escalation agreements, he added, are built through continued dialogue with all relevant states and actors, saying Washington continues to believe that "restraint and engagement represent the most constructive path".
Barrack called on all sides to prioritise "reasoned dialogue" over further military incidents.
His comments came as Damascus issued its own sharply worded condemnation, describing the Israeli attack as an "unjustified aggression" and a flagrant violation of Syrian sovereignty.
Syria's Foreign Ministry said the strikes represented "a dangerous escalation that threatens security and stability in the region".
It said the continued Israeli attacks since the fall of Bashar al-Assad on 8 December 2024 were taking place despite Syria exercising restraint and seeking to consolidate stability and avoid escalation.
The ministry accused Israel of attempting to undermine those efforts and "drag the region towards further tension and instability".
Damascus called on the international community and UN Security Council to clearly condemn the attack and take a "firm position towards repeated Israeli violations of Syrian sovereignty".
Syria, it added, would continue to defend its rights and national interests through legitimate means permitted under international law.
During Syria's civil war, opposition forces captured Abu al-Duhur in September 2015. The Assad regime regained control of the airport in 2018 and held it until Bashar al-Assad was ousted in December 2024.
Israel targets Syria's military capabilities
Since the fall of the Assad regime, Israel has stepped up its raids and incursions into Syria, while targeting much of the country's remaining military infrastructure.
Israeli attacks have struck Syrian air-defence systems, long- and medium-range missiles, weapons and missile depots, scientific research centres and other military facilities.
Israeli strikes have also hit several key Syrian airfields and military installations, including Hama airport, as well as Tiyas, Shayrat, Palmyra, Dumayr and Mezzeh airfields.
Syria's naval fleets at the ports of Latakia and Tartus have also been targeted, even as the country's new authorities have begun taking steps to rebuild the military and its air capabilities.
Last month, Syrian state media reported that Israeli forces had carried out a fresh incursion into southern Syria, despite a visiting UN chief demanding an end to Israeli violations.
The Syrian state news agency SANA said Israeli soldiers, accompanied by three military vehicles and a bulldozer, had established a checkpoint in al-Aarada. Israeli forces also dropped leaflets in nearby towns warning residents against closing roads.
The strikes on Abu al-Duhur mark the first time the airport has been targeted since the fall of the Assad regime.

FIFA confirms COO Kevin Lamour 'has left' after criticising Infantino's World Cup plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:12:04 UTC
18:12:04 KST

The senior FIFA executive had warned speaking out against Infantino's controversial investment plan could cost him his job.
FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour has left his role less than three weeks after publicly attacking Gianni Infantino's plan to bring private investors into world football's biggest competitions.
FIFA confirmed Lamour's employment ended on 17 August but did not give a reason for his departure. Some media outlets are claiming he had been sacked.
"FIFA thanks Kevin for his two years of service and wishes him the best of luck for the future," a FIFA spokesperson told AFP, confirming "the working relationship between FIFA and Kevin Lamour as FIFA's chief operating officer has ended".
Lamour had been one of FIFA's most senior executives since joining from European governing body UEFA in November 2024. His responsibilities included overseeing finance, legal and compliance, communications, member associations, technology and operations and social responsibility across FIFA's offices in Zurich, Paris and Miami.
But he publicly broke with Infantino over the proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a new commercial subsidiary to be valued at around $20 billion (€17bn) to run its major tournaments - including the World Cup - and allow private investors to acquire a 20% stake.
Lamour accused FIFA's administration of being "deceived" over how the proposal was developed and described FFE as "the project of one person".
"Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."
"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," Lamour said in a statement on July 31.
His departure follows the resignation of Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro last month, a former US Soccer president and Goldman Sachs executive.
Cordeiro said he had not been involved in developing FFE and described the proposal as "a bad deal for football", questioning why FIFA needed to raise billions from outside investors when it had significant reserves and no debt.
Infantino subsequently abandoned FFE following widespread opposition when three regional football governing bodies – UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and Caribbean) and the AFC (Asia) – said his plan was a "fundamental breach of trust" with the institutions the body was designed to serve.
FIFA released a statement on 8 August in which it said, "It is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President."

Kravchenko: 10 officials of Odesa’s district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center detained on suspicion of torture
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:11:30 EEST
18:11:30 KST

Kravchenko: 10 officials of Odesa’s district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center detained on suspicion of torture
Kyiv • UNN
The Prosecutor General reported that ten servicemen of one of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers in Odesa had been notified of suspicion. They are suspected of unlawful deprivation of liberty and torture. At least eight victims have been identified.
Ten service members of one of the district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers in Odesa have been notified of suspicion of unlawfully depriving citizens of their liberty and torturing them. The suspects have been detained. This was reported by Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, UNN writes.
"Mobilization is an obligation. Torture is a crime. Today, ten service members of one of the district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers in Odesa were notified of suspicion of unlawfully depriving citizens of their liberty and torturing them," the Prosecutor General said.
The suspects have been detained. The issue of choosing preventive measures is being decided.
According to the investigation, for several months they unlawfully detained people, used tear gas, beat them, and forcibly took them to the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center. In one episode, a man was hit by an official vehicle in order to detain him. Another man was strangled, beaten, handcuffed, and, under threats, forced to provide his phone password.
According to Kravchenko, at least eight victims have been identified so far.
"There is one more detail. Seven of the ten suspects were mobilized in the spring of 2025 and immediately sent to serve at an Odesa Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center. The state gave them uniforms, authority, and responsibility. According to the investigation, they used this authority to unlawfully commit violence against people," the Prosecutor General wrote.
Ruslan Kravchenko emphasized that mobilization is necessary for the country's defense, but the need for it does not give anyone the right to violate the law.
"Ukraine is at war. Our military personnel have been on the front line for years and need reinforcements. Mobilization is necessary for the defense of the state, while evasion, corruption, and illegal schemes for obtaining deferments must receive an appropriate legal assessment. The need for mobilization does not give anyone the right to violate the law.
Therefore, the prosecutor's office's position is simple: we do not divide people by uniform, position, or status: those who evade fulfilling their duty to the state must be held accountable under the law. And those who use unlawful violence on behalf of the state must be held accountable in the same way," the Prosecutor General emphasized.

For 10th day, Israeli occupiers maintain tight siege on Palestinian families in Qusra

Qais Omar Darwesh and Lina Altawell
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
Israeli occupiers continued Tuesday to maintain a tight siege for the 10th day on three Palestinian homes in the town of Qusra, south of Nablus in the northern occupied West Bank, under Israeli army protection, a local official said.
Since Aug. 9, occupiers have laid a siege around three Palestinian families, comprising around 13 people, in the Ras al-Ain area of the town, obstructing the delivery of food, water and basic supplies.
Qusra Mayor Abdul Azim al-Wadi told Anadolu that Israeli forces and occupiers continued to surround the three homes, preventing families from entering or leaving, as the area has been declared a “closed military zone.”
“The occupiers are deployed in the area and move freely,” he said.
Wadi said the owner of one of the homes, Louay Abu Rida, a US citizen, managed Monday to reach his home, accompanied by an American delegation.
“It was very difficult to see your home and family besieged through surveillance cameras, and the hardest part was that I was far away from them and unable to reach them,” Abu Rida told Anadolu after his arrival in the town.
He said that as soon as he arrived in the town from the US, the scenes he had been watching remotely had become a reality around his home, with occupiers reaching the vicinity despite the presence of the Israeli army in the area.
“We were told the army was there to protect us and keep the occupiers away, but what we saw on the ground was different,” Abu Rida said.
The Ras al-Ain area has seen repeated attacks by occupiers in recent months to establish an illegal settlement outpost and seize Palestinian land and homes. Palestinians have warned that the siege could become a tool to displace residents and take over their property.
Separately, a Palestinian was injured by Israeli army fire in Al-Ram town, north of occupied East Jerusalem, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent Society.
Israeli soldiers opened fire at a Palestinian near the separation wall in Al-Ram, witnesses said. The circumstances of the shooting remain unclear.
The shooting came amid escalating attacks by the Israeli army and occupiers across the West Bank since the Gaza war in October 2023, killing more than 1,100 people, according to Palestinian figures.

Pakistan top court orders Imran Khan moved from jail to hospital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:11:00 UTC
18:11:00 KST

Pakistan top court orders ex-PM Khan moved to hospital
August 18, 2026
Pakistan's Supreme Court on Tuesday ordered that jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan be moved to hospital for medical checks after his lawyers filed a petition citing poor health.
The top court said the 73-year-old would be transferred to Shifa International hospital in the capital, Islamabad, within two days.
The cricketer-turned-politician was jailed in 2023 after being convicted on a string of charges that he claims were politically motivated.
Khan's party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), and his family have repeatedly raised fears about his health in prison. His lawyers have also stated that he has lost most of the vision in his right eye.
Khan ally welcomes decision
Tuesday's order came after a medical team examined Khan at Rawalpnidi's Adiala jail last week, where it recorded high blood pressure, palpitations and anxiety.
"It's a very welcome order and we wish it had happened sooner so his eye and general health would not have deteriorated this much," Sayed Zulfikar Bukhari, a close Khan aide, said in a statement.
"He should remain in hospital until all doctors are satisfied," he added.
Khan's spokesperson said he was expected to remain in hospital until September 16.
Why is Khan in jail?
Khan was Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022. Following his ouster in a no-confidence vote, he was convicted on a number of charges including allegations of an unlawful marriage and corruption. He was sentenced late last year, along with his wife, to 17 years in prison for graft.
Both deny wrongdoing.
PTI still enjoys significant support across key provinces in Pakistan, and Khan himself remains a popular figure. His arrest in early 2023 triggered nationwide protests that resulted in hundreds of people being arrested.
Earlier this year, cricket greats from around the world appealed to the Pakistani government for Khan to receive proper medical treatment in prison, calling in a letter for "decency and justice."

Zambia's election marred by irregularities and 'militia' arrests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:11:00 UTC
18:11:00 KST

Zambia election marred by irregularities, 'militia' arrests
August 18, 2026
Zambia's government announced on Sunday that police had arrested 11 people, including six opposition figures, in a raid against "militia activity." The arrests took place on Thursday night, according to a government statement.
"The individuals in issue were found in possession of high-grade military weapons, ammunition and other materials for use in armed insurrection," it said.
Zambia's main opposition party, the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Progress (NRPUP), said shots were fired in the raid, which took place at the home of its presidential candidate Brian Mundubile, as Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported.
The party said it "rejects with absolute disdain the spurious and entirely false claims made by the Zambian Government that the NRPUP, its leadership or its members have been involved in insurgency, militia activity or any related conduct whatsoever."
Mundubile added that heavily armed personnel had raided his residence after the election in what he described as an attack on his life.
He also claimed on social media that he was interrogated by army officers over videos he had released, and that he suffered mistreatment while in custody — accusations denied by the authorities.
The government has responded that those claims were "unsubstantiated," with outgoing Foreign Affairs Minister Mulambo Haimbe telling DW that "the individuals that have been apprehended have been charged, first of all, and will face trial."
"So, it is not Mr. Mundubile's place to make assertions on matters that will go through a court process," Haimbe stressed, adding that any actions taken by authorities were to make sure that the "security of the nation is not compromised" during the election process.
Concerns raised during Zambia vote counting
The arrests come amid an intensely contested election: The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) suspended vote counting for around six hours on Friday following reports of violence perpetrated against polling staff and the alleged theft of ballot papers.
The count resumed after the commission announced that the "security threat" had eventually been contained, AFP reported.
Mundubile argued that this suspension created opportunities for interference and manipulation of results, while the ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) rejected the claims, saying Mundubile was attempting to undermine public confidence in the electoral process.
Opposition figures have said, however, that the concerns extend beyond the pause in the vote count.
In a statement, Makebi Zulu, vice presidential candidate of the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance, alleged a broader pattern of interference involving electoral officials, missing polling documents, security force involvement and intimidation of opposition actors.
"A climate of fear cannot produce a free and fair election," Zulu warned.
Bishops demand accountability
Similar concerns have also been raised by Zambia's Conference of Catholic Bishops, which called on the electoral commission to "account fully and publicly for the chain of custody of every affected ballot box and ballot paper."
The group of bishops, which wields considerable influence in the country, further urged authorities to ensure that any military deployment remain limited, transparent and temporary.
They also expressed concern over reports of harassment and the alleged detention of opposition officials by armed officers, calling for full transparency over the whereabouts of anyone held by authorities.
"Any person held by state agencies must be promptly accounted for, granted access to legal counsel and family, and either charged according to law or released," the bishops said.
EU observers: Election campaign held in 'a constrained democratic space'
International observers from the European Union and the Southern African Development Community (SADC) also voiced their concerns about aspects of the electoral process, including mounting reports of intimidation and tensions surrounding the vote count.
SADC warned that the suspension of vote counting had generated "uncertainty and anxiety" among voters and political stakeholders.
The EU Election Observation Mission raised similar concerns, saying the campaign had been held in a "constrained democratic space," also citing reports of intimidation of opposition candidates, disruptions to some rallies, late changes to electoral laws and an uneven playing field, which it said favored the ruling party.
EU chief observer Michael McNamara also pointed to incumbency advantages and heavily pro-government state media coverage, arguing that key democratic freedoms had been restricted during the campaign.
Legacy of Edgar Lungu
This increasingly polarized political landscape in Zambia is shaped largely by the last transfer of power, which brought President Hakainde Hichilema to office in 2021 after his victory over former President Edgar Lungu.
Since then, supporters of the former ruling Patriotic Front (PF) have accused the government of targeting Lungu allies through arrests and investigations, while the government has argued it is pursuing accountability after years of alleged corruption and abuse of power under the PF administration.
Lungu died in South Africa last year, resulting in growing veneration among his followers and supporters.
Cabinet Secretary Patrick Kangwa meanwhile said those taken into custody during the raids also included Patrick Mwansa, the husband of Lungu's daughter Tasila, who he said was being held at a police station in Lusaka.
Optimism while waiting for final results
The election results have stirred a mix of hope, anxiety and strong reactions among Zambians.
Gracious Kaoma, a political science student at the University of Zambia, said she was "very hopeful yet concerned" about the election "because the process has been unusually long and very challenging."
She added that the violence surrounding the vote had been "painful to watch." Kaoma nevertheless expressed hope that Zambia's political leaders would "reconcile and put Zambia's needs first."
Haimbe echoed those sentiments, telling DW that Zambia is "a bastion of democracy on the African continent, and it is our intention as the UPND administration of President Hakainde Hichilema to grow from strength to strength in that regard."
Meanwhile, Lusaka resident Lydia Zulu also expressed support for the incumbent leader, saying she was "happy that the elections have gone on peacefully and well. Because I have seen President Hakainde Hichilema is leading, I'm happy that he's coming back."
Final results are yet to be released, but according to the official tally, Hichilema appears to have widened his lead: Electoral commission figures from 70 of 226 constituencies show the incumbent ahead with 626,434 votes to challenger Mundubile's 505,795 — a margin of more than 120,000 votes.
While the outcome remains undecided for now, Mundubile has repeated his allegation of widespread irregularities, claiming victory based on his party's own vote count.
Electoral authorities, however, have rejected those claims, stressing that only the electoral commission can officially declare the election result.
Additional reporting by Kathy Short in Lusaka.
Editors: Keith Walker and Sertan Sanderson

Mundubile argued that this suspension created opportunities for interference and manipulation of results, while the ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) rejected the claims, saying Mundubile was attempting to undermine public confidence in the electoral process.
Opposition figures have said, however, that the concerns extend beyond the pause in the vote count.
In a statement, Makebi Zulu, vice presidential candidate of the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance, alleged a broader pattern of interference involving electoral officials, missing polling documents, security force involvement and intimidation of opposition actors.
"A climate of fear cannot produce a free and fair election," Zulu warned.
Bishops demand accountability
Similar concerns have also been raised by Zambia's Conference of Catholic Bishops, which called on the electoral commission to "account fully and publicly for the chain of custody of every affected ballot box and ballot paper."
The group of bishops, which wields considerable influence in the country, further urged authorities to ensure that any military deployment remain limited, transparent and temporary.
They also expressed concern over reports of harassment and the alleged detention of opposition officials by armed officers, calling for full transparency over the whereabouts of anyone held by authorities.
"Any person held by state agencies must be promptly accounted for, granted access to legal counsel and family, and either charged according to law or released," the bishops said.
EU observers: Election campaign held in 'a constrained democratic space'
International observers from the European Union and the Southern African Development Community (SADC) also voiced their concerns about aspects of the electoral process, including mounting reports of intimidation and tensions surrounding the vote count.
SADC warned that the suspension of vote counting had generated "uncertainty and anxiety" among voters and political stakeholders.
The EU Election Observation Mission raised similar concerns, saying the campaign had been held in a "constrained democratic space," also citing reports of intimidation of opposition candidates, disruptions to some rallies, late changes to electoral laws and an uneven playing field, which it said favored the ruling party.
EU chief observer Michael McNamara also pointed to incumbency advantages and heavily pro-government state media coverage, arguing that key democratic freedoms had been restricted during the campaign.
Legacy of Edgar Lungu
This increasingly polarized political landscape in Zambia is shaped largely by the last transfer of power, which brought President Hakainde Hichilema to office in 2021 after his victory over former President Edgar Lungu.
Since then, supporters of the former ruling Patriotic Front (PF) have accused the government of targeting Lungu allies through arrests and investigations, while the government has argued it is pursuing accountability after years of alleged corruption and abuse of power under the PF administration.
Lungu died in South Africa last year, resulting in growing veneration among his followers and supporters.
Cabinet Secretary Patrick Kangwa meanwhile said those taken into custody during the raids also included Patrick Mwansa, the husband of Lungu's daughter Tasila, who he said was being held at a police station in Lusaka.
Optimism while waiting for final results
The election results have stirred a mix of hope, anxiety and strong reactions among Zambians.
Gracious Kaoma, a political science student at the University of Zambia, said she was "very hopeful yet concerned" about the election "because the process has been unusually long and very challenging."
She added that the violence surrounding the vote had been "painful to watch." Kaoma nevertheless expressed hope that Zambia's political leaders would "reconcile and put Zambia's needs first."
Haimbe echoed those sentiments, telling DW that Zambia is "a bastion of democracy on the African continent, and it is our intention as the UPND administration of President Hakainde Hichilema to grow from strength to strength in that regard."
Meanwhile, Lusaka resident Lydia Zulu also expressed support for the incumbent leader, saying she was "happy that the elections have gone on peacefully and well. Because I have seen President Hakainde Hichilema is leading, I'm happy that he's coming back."
Final results are yet to be released, but according to the official tally, Hichilema appears to have widened his lead: Electoral commission figures from 70 of 226 constituencies show the incumbent ahead with 626,434 votes to challenger Mundubile's 505,795 — a margin of more than 120,000 votes.
While the outcome remains undecided for now, Mundubile has repeated his allegation of widespread irregularities, claiming victory based on his party's own vote count.
Electoral authorities, however, have rejected those claims, stressing that only the electoral commission can officially declare the election result.
Additional reporting by Kathy Short in Lusaka.
Editors: Keith Walker and Sertan Sanderson

Copper tests new record amid AI and energy demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:09:56 UTC
18:09:56 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu, Emirhan Yilmaz, and Emir Yildirim
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
Copper reached a new record, rising as high as $6.73 per pound on Monday due to strong artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investments, growing renewable energy demand and cost pressures further exacerbated by Middle East tensions.
Copper prices have continued to trend upward since last year, and the base metal has gained more than 18% this year amid accelerating global investments in data centers, energy infrastructure and power transmission systems. Expectations of stronger industrial production activity also drove up copper prices.
Supply constraints also contributed to the rise in copper as disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and resulting issues in the sulfur supply chain affected copper production, fueling supply concerns. The combination of strong demand and supply-side issues drove copper to historic highs.
Slowing US inflation and rising concerns over the country’s economic growth eased hawkish expectations for the Fed’s future monetary policy decisions, providing upward support for commodity prices.
Copper later stabilized at $6.56 per pound.
Zafer Ergezen, a futures and commodities expert, told Anadolu that copper is one of the commodities with the highest demand, primarily due to AI investments, while other sectors like electric vehicles (EVs) and the global energy sector are major drivers.
“Reports consistently show a supply shortage in this area, so even if supply increases, the demand would grow at a much stronger rate,” he said.
Ergezen stated that US tariffs and the US-Israel-Iran conflict have been instrumental in the rise in copper prices, as mounting logistics and energy costs due to Middle East tensions increased prices across the entire mining sector.
“The most significant increase in demand for copper comes from the AI sector, and we’ve seen this particularly rapidly in China,” he said.
“We’re seeing massive investments, one-time deals worth $100 billion being signed in the AI sector, and these will continue in the coming period, which means copper demand will continue to rise and remain strong, meaning copper prices will continue climbing,” he added.
Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Capital, said the intense supply competition between the US and China pushed copper above $6.70 per pound, while major copper producers struggled to meet their production targets.

Jobs to go at Ferguson Marine shipyard in Port Glasgow
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
10:07:45 BST
18:07:45 KST

Ferguson Marine has opened a voluntary redundancy programme expected to see up to 70 employees leave the Port Glasgow yard, as work on the ferry Glen Rosa winds down and before contracts for four new vessels are finalised, the company stated.
The yard is moving into the final outfitting and commissioning phases of Glen Rosa ahead of delivery in the fourth quarter of 2026, and says the workload is naturally reducing as a result. Formal consultation has begun.
Graeme Thomson, chief executive of Ferguson Marine, said: “Our immediate focus remains the safe, high-quality handover of Glen Rosa in Q4 2026. However, as the vessel nears completion, we face an inevitable gap in workload while we work with the Scottish Government to make the relevant preparations to enable us to proceed with contract negotiations.
“Shipbuilding capability relies on continuity and while changes of this nature are difficult, taking proactive action now ensures we protect the long-term viability of the yard and remain lean, modern, and ready to cut steel on the new fleet as quickly as possible.”
He said: “We take our responsibility to our workforce and community incredibly seriously. By offering a voluntary redundancy path, we want to support team members who have given so much to shipbuilding on the Clyde as they consider their next steps. At the same time, we are doing everything in our power to ensure the yard is structured to offer secure, long-term careers once the new build programme gets underway.”
The Scottish Government announced in March 2026 that it intended to make a strategic direct award to Ferguson Marine covering four vessels: two ferries for Caledonian Maritime Assets under the Small Vessel Replacement Programme, along with a marine protection vessel and a marine research vessel. Due diligence on that award is still under way.
Ferguson Marine says the changes announced are designed to address the size of the business and align skills across the yard so it is ready to begin work as soon as the contracts are settled, and that the consultation will not affect the remaining work or the delivery schedule for Glen Rosa. A phased transition plan is in place across active projects.
GMB Scotland, the largest union at the yard, called the job losses a betrayal of a blameless workforce and blamed ministers for failing to deliver new contracts while sending work overseas.
Louise Gilmour, GMB Scotland secretary, said 70 jobs are at risk while the Scottish Government refuses to sign off contracts promised before the Holyrood election in May.
She said: “Shipbuilders needs ships to build so where are those promised to Ferguson Marine? If they ever come, who will build them? Fergusons was once Scotland’s ferry factory with a worldwide reputation for excellence and should be again.
“Instead, skilled and experienced shipbuilders are being encouraged to leave as those in charge send contracts everywhere but here. The lack of support, ambition and industrial strategy is abject.”
Ms Gilmour, who noted that a third of CalMac’s current fleet was built at the yard, tied the losses to a long-standing failure to open a pipeline of work after Glen Rosa and Glen Sannox.
She said: “Its reputation has been battered for ten years because of two calamitous contracts decided and driven by those in charge of our ferry network. Their hubris and incompetence have failed a blameless workforce that deserves the chance to turn the page.”
Glen Rosa is the second of two dual-fuel ferries ordered for the Clyde and Hebrides network in 2015, a contract that ran years late and far over budget, and which led to the yard being taken into public ownership in December 2019 after Ferguson Marine Engineering went into administration. Her sister ship Glen Sannox was handed over in early 2025, around seven years behind the original schedule.
The pattern the redundancies illustrate is the one that has dogged smaller British yards for decades. A yard that finishes one order without another already cut in steel loses the people who built the first, and the welders, pipefitters and outfitters who leave rarely come back. Ferguson Marine is arguing that shrinking now protects its ability to staff up when the new programme starts.
The yard also carries out fabrication work for BAE Systems on the Type 26 frigate programme, producing structural units that are shipped up the river to Govan for assembly, and is partway through a transformation project intended to modernise the site.
Ferguson Marine has operated at Port Glasgow since 1903 and is the last commercial shipbuilder on the lower Clyde.

Campaigners call for Amsterdam to pull plug on giant data centre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
09:07:39 UTC
18:07:39 KST

Campaigners call for Amsterdam to pull plug on giant data centre
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
More than 500 people have joined a campaign to stop a huge data centre being built in Amsterdam-Zuid, arguing that it will bring “zero benefits to the area”.
The Dutch government has introduced restrictions on the size of data centres in recent years following criticism from provincial and municipal governments about the strain on the electricity network. Data centres accounted for 4.6% of all electricity use in the Netherlands in 2024.
But the plans to build a 24,000 m2 facility on Amsterdam’s Science Park were submitted by US firm Equinix before the ban, which only applies to new developments, took effect in 2022.
Local residents have also become increasingly vocal in opposing the construction of data centres, while campaign groups Geef Tegengas and Extinction Rebellion both staged demonstrations this summer against a Microsoft project in Amsterdam Sloterdijk.
“There are already enough data centres to keep everything running. This is becoming overkill,” Dylan Bakker of Stop Datacenter Zuidoost told NOS.
Amsterdam city council, which wants to build 8,000 homes in Zuidoost to help relieve the national housing shortage, has attached extra conditions to the site, such as requiring the residual heat from the plant to be used for domestic heating.
Water and electricity
There are also concerns about the strain on water supplies, which have been exacerbated by the summer drought. Equinix said in its planning application that it would need 274 million litres of water a year for the first stage of the project, rising to more than a billion litres when the data centre is complete in 2036.
But the municipality says it would face legal action and penalties if it tore up the permit to build the data center at this stage.
Equinix has said it will only build one of four planned 60-metre data towers initially, until electricity grid operator Tennet can supply enough power.
Tennet warned earlier this year that the network was nearing capacity, leading to a six-month moratorium on new connections in Utrecht.
The complete campus in Zuidoost will consume 779 kWh of electricity a year, almost as much as all the households Amsterdam combined, which currently use 869 kWh.
Michiel Eielts, director of Equinix Benelux, argued that the data centres were an essential part of modern infrastructure. “Every house needs the internet. We need data centres for the growth of our companies, our public services and our security,” he said.

DUSHANBE, August 18. /TASS/. Servicemen from a sniper rifle company of the 201st Russian Guards Military Base, stationed in Tajikistan, practiced neutralizing a simulated enemy at the Lyaur mountain training range during a live-fire exercise, the press service of the Central Military District reported.
It said that according to the exercise scenario, unmanned aerial vehicle crews detected a concentration of "enemy" forces in one of the mountain gorges during aerial reconnaissance and transmitted the data to the command post. Snipers, having received the order to neutralize the targets, moved on foot to the designated area and then established primary and backup positions for observation and firing, using improvised and specialized camouflage equipment.
"After detecting the ‘targets’ and determining firing positions, the service members engaged the targets at ranges from 300 to 1,000 meters in sniper pairs. Fire was conducted using SVD, SVD-M, SVD-K, and SV-98 sniper rifles," the statement said.
The Central Military District’s press service emphasized that the exercise was conducted taking into account experience gained in the Russian special military operations in Ukraine, as well as the specific features of mountainous terrain. "The service members practiced engaging targets from various cover positions, including from simulated urban structures, adjusting their fire based on elevation angles," according to the statement.
The 201st Russian military base stationed in Tajikistan is Russia’s largest military facility outside its borders. Located in two cities, Dushanbe and Bokhtar, it includes motorized rifle, tank, artillery, reconnaissance, air defense, NBC defense troops and communications units.
